abstract: To enhance learning and training, VR haptic devices must provide safe and physically accurate feedback that helps users build intuitions about force and motion. We present SafeForce, a method for rendering force feedback by capturing user input and reconfiguring a compliant mechanism in real time to align perceived with expected forces. We implemented SafeForce in a grounded Encountered-Type Haptic Display (ETHD) and demonstrated its versatility through three representative physics scenarios: pushing a stationary object, experiencing electrostatic repulsion, and bouncing a moving object. A user study with 29 participants showed that users adapted to new interaction profiles within 2-3 trials, and that rendered forces remained within perceptual thresholds except in the heaviest and most dynamic conditions. These results suggest that SafeForce enables rapid, perceptually aligned, and educationally valuable interactions with moving virtual objects.

abstract: Virtual reality (VR) applications face a critical trade-off: while visual immersion is the core experience, it often induces cybersickness (CS), leading to user attrition. Existing visual interventions (e.g., field-of-view restriction) alleviate discomfort at the cost of compromising immersion. Auditory interventions have been widely applied in mitigating motion sickness (MS), such as through music interventions and synchronized sound effects. Among all MS mitigation approaches, anticipatory audio cues have demonstrated effectiveness in vehicular MS contexts, reducing symptoms by approximately 17%. However, questions remain regarding VR cybersickness (CS): Do anticipatory audio cues remain effective in highly immersive virtual environments, where the dominance of visual interaction in VR may alter cue perception compared to that in MS contexts? How can VR motion intensity information be encoded, given that such information is largely absent in current mitigation strategies? How can anticipatory audio cues be systematically designed for CS mitigation through explicit mapping frameworks that link visual motion parameters to audio features? To address these gaps, this study establishes an optical flow mapping framework that encodes motion direction through stereo positioning and intensity through temporal patterns, delivering the results 2 seconds in advance. A within-subjects experiment (N = 24) was conducted in VR roller coaster environments, in which four conditions were compared. Results demonstrated a significant reduction in cybersickness across all audio conditions (direction-only: d = 0.862; intensity-only: d = 0.670; combined: d = 1.497, p < .001), with combined cues outperforming single-dimension alternatives (p < .016). All interventions preserved visual immersion (M ≈ 4.0/5) and maintained high usability metrics. This framework demonstrates that non-visual predictive cues can address the immersion-comfort trade-off in VR applications.

abstract: Virtual Reality offers highly immersive experiences, yet users remain physically situated in real-world environments whose layouts often differ from the virtual spaces they perceive. In these settings, users’ spatial memory of the physical environment may interact with or even conflict with the virtual scene, potentially influencing locomotion, task performance, and situational awareness. Despite its importance, the influence of physical space memory on VR interaction remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we conducted three controlled studies that varied the virtual scene and task structure to examine how physical-space memory affects VR performance. In Study I, participants interacted with virtual props placed at different distances from real obstacles, returning to a fixed start point after each trial to isolate the effect of obstacle proximity on immediate strategies. Study II used the same setup but removed the resets, allowing us to observe how memory reliance changes as task duration increases. In Study III, we introduced virtual anchors with varying degrees of alignment to physical landmarks, assessing how spatial similarity between the two spaces influences navigation and task efficiency. Our findings reveal that users subconsciously adapt their navigation and decision-making based on remembered surroundings, even when no visual cues are available. These insights deepen our understanding of spatial cognition in immersive VR and provide actionable guidelines for designing safer, more efficient, and cognitively consistent virtual environments.

abstract: Collaborative tasks in Virtual Reality, such as jointly manipulating objects, require tight multi-user synchronization. However, users often operate in heterogeneous physical environments with varying room sizes, furniture layouts, and obstacles. Enforcing a single, globally consistent virtual scene across such diversity constrains users’ natural movements, underutilizes available physical space, and ultimately degrades collaboration efficiency. We present CoVR, a novel framework that enables seamless multi-user collaboration in VR across heterogeneous physical spaces by prioritizing interaction alignment over strict spatial alignment. Instead of requiring all users to share an identical virtual scene, CoVR provides each user with a personalized virtual scene layout while maintaining synchronized actions and consistent collaborative outcomes. Technically, we formulate a multi-user coupled optimization problem that jointly optimizes per-user layouts to maximize usable space and facilitate seamless task execution. A key challenge arises from bi-directional dependencies: one user’s optimized layout determines feasible trajectories, which in turn constrain other users’ optimizations, and vice versa. To tackle this, CoVR introduces an iterative joint optimization algorithm alternating between personalized scene refinement and cross-user synchronization until convergence. We evaluate CoVR across typical collaborative tasks. Results show that CoVR significantly outperforms conventional scene alignment methods, leading to notable improvements in spatial efficiency, task completion time, and user comfort. These findings underscore its potential for scalable, natural, and efficient multi-user VR collaboration.

abstract: High-quality facial animation retargeting is crucial in digital entertainment production, enabling the transfer of animations from a source rig to a target rig. To avoid the need of manual transfer, automatic retargeting methods can be employed. However, creating universal methods remains challenging due to varying rig and topologies. We propose a novel retargeting method based on the idea that any facial expression can be decomposed into a weighted sum of Facial Action Coding System (FACS) poses. Our method assumes that these decompositions transfer across rigs with minimal need of refinement. We utilize a machine learning model to extract FACS weights from source frames. This model is trained solely on source animation data, requiring no target data or complex correspondence mappings. After a refinement step, these weights are then applied to the target rig’s FACS poses. Our technique supports seamless animation transfer across different rigs while allowing for artistic modifications by adjusting individual FACS poses. Our experiments demonstrate that this method produces high-quality retargeted animations and outperforms other retargeting methods. We explore how different design choices impact retargeting quality and showcase artistic control of asymmetries. By simplifying the workflow for rigged heads, this flexible framework enhances production efficiency while maintaining artistic control.

abstract: Over the past two decades, researchers have made significant steps in simulating agent-based human crowds, yet most efforts remain focused on low-level tasks such as collision avoidance, path following, and flocking. As a result, these approaches often struggle to capture the high-level behaviors that emerge from sustained agent-agent and agent-environment interactions over time. We introduce Generative LLM-Informed Modeling for Characters (GLIMC), a generative framework that produces crowd scenarios capturing agent–agent and agent–environment interactions, shaping coherent high-level crowd plans. To avoid the labor-intensive process of collecting and annotating real crowd video data, we leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to bootstrap synthetic datasets of crowd scenarios. To represent those scenarios, we propose a time-expanded graph structure encoding actions, interactions, and spatial context. GLIMC employs a dual Variational Graph Autoencoder (VGAE) architecture that jointly learns connectivity patterns and node features conditioned on textual and structural signals, overcoming the limitations of direct LLM generation to enable scalable, environment-aware multi-agent crowd simulations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on scenarios with diverse behaviors such as, a University Campus and a Train Station, showing that it generates heterogeneous crowds, coherent interactions, and high-level decision-making patterns consistent with the provided context.

abstract: The generation of consistent multi-view images is essential for diffusion-based 3D texture synthesis, a key component of modern 3D content pipelines. However, existing methods remain weakly coupled across viewpoints, often exhibiting inconsistencies between views that result in artifacts such as ghosting, misalignment, and texture distortions. We introduce PixelSync, a training-free mechanism that explicitly enforces multi-view consistency during the diffusion process. Our method operates in two stages. First, we compute visibility-aware pixel correspondences between known views in a fast pre-computation step by utilizing geometric information obtained from a given 3D model. Then, during the diffusion process, we enforce consistency through two complementary algorithms: (i) attention synchronization, by modifying the attention scores in the U-Net’s down- and mid-blocks, and (ii) latent synchronization, by progressively aligning features on their corresponding shared pixels. PixelSync can be seamlessly integrated into pre-trained diffusion models without retraining, offering a lightweight and effective solution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for generative texture synthesis by plugging PixelSync into established multi-view diffusion backbones, showcasing reduced cross-view artifacts and improved global coherence across standard quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) are increasingly being used as tools to map coordinates to signals, encompassing applications from neural fields to texture compression, shape representations, and beyond. Most INR methods are based on using high-dimensional projections of the initial coordinates through encoders such as grid or positional encoding. Nevertheless, positional encoding is often insufficient and grids, as we show in this paper, require high resolution for being able to learn. In this paper, we demonstrate that positional encoding can be used not only as a high-dimensional embedding but also decomposed as a series of meaningful points. We propose the Positional Encoding Coordinate System, where we treat the projection of the original coordinate at each frequency as a point of interest. We describe the motion of each point with respect to the frequencies and show that it follows a unique pattern. Finally, we use the unique motion of each point as a basis decomposition for doing learned positional encoding using grids. We prove, using three competitive applications— image representation, texture compression, and signed distance function—that the proposed approach outperforms the current state of the art methods, and often requires 25% less parameters for equivalent reconstruction error or rendering.

abstract: 3D Aesthetics is significant in digital design, shaping how users experience real-time 3D content in games, VR, and product design. However, creating aesthetically pleasing shapes remains challenging due to diverse subjective standards and the lack of tools that support aesthetics-driven editing. Users often rely on intuition without explicit guidance on visual appeal, making aesthetic refinement slow, inconsistent, and cognitively demanding, particularly in fast-paced, iterative workflows. To address this challenge, we conducted in-depth interviews with design experts to identify challenges in aesthetics-oriented modeling workflows. Based on the findings, we developed Aesthetic3D, a 3D modeling interface offering real-time aesthetic scores learned from human perceptual data. Furthermore, Aesthetic3D seamlessly integrates the learned aesthetic measure into intuitive editing operations, enabling aesthetics-driven exploration and refinement of shape geometry. We evaluated Aesthetic3D through an ablation study, an open-ended study, and two generalization evaluations. Comprehensive experiments show that with Aesthetic3D, users can easily and effectively enhance the aesthetic appeal of 3D shapes.

abstract: Intrinsic decomposition — which expresses image colors as the product of diffuse albedo and shading, possibly augmented with view-dependent residuals — has a long history in image editing as it enables the modification of object colors and textures without altering lighting. We extend intrinsic decomposition to radiance fields represented with Gaussian splatting by proposing solutions to three key aspects of such decomposition. First, we describe how to model the intrinsic decomposition as independent sets of Gaussian primitives, which allows each set to adapt to the characteristics of the layer it represents. Second, we present an optimization procedure guided by data-driven predictions to disentangle multi-view photographs of a scene into the aforementioned intrinsic sets. Finally, we provide an editing workflow where users modify the texture of planar surfaces simply by modifying the albedo of that surface in one image. Capturing this edit within the intrinsic radiance field allows re-rendering of the edited scene with plausible lighting under arbitrary viewpoints.

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of unpaired shape translation on 3D point clouds. While prior methods typically rely on global latent vectors or spatially structured grids, such representations often lack the flexibility to capture both semantic structures and fine-grained geometric details. To address this, we propose operating directly in a structured token space, where tokens are pretrained through masked auto encoding. Unlike rigid spatial grids that impose fixed layouts, our tokens naturally adapt to geometric variations while maintaining semantic coherence. This structured yet flexible latent space enables semantically meaningful and geometrically precise transformations. A transformer-based translator is proposed to manipulate these tokens. This gated dual-branch translator enables detail-preserving and topology-aware shape translation across categories. Experiments on challenging tasks, such as chair-to-table transformations, demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in preserving both global structure and part-level details.

abstract: Algorithms leveraging ReSTIR-style spatiotemporal reuse have recently proliferated, hugely increasing effective sample count for light transport in real-time ray and path tracers. Many papers have been published on novel theoretical improvements, but algorithmic improvements and engineering insights toward optimal implementation have largely been neglected. We demonstrate enhancements to ReSTIR PT that make it 2–3x faster, decrease both visual and numerical error, and improve its robustness, making it closer to production-ready. We halve the spatial reuse cost by reciprocal neighbor selection, robustify shift mappings with new footprint-based reconnection criteria, and reduce spatiotemporal correlation with duplication maps. We further improve both performance and quality by extensive optimization, unifying direct and global illumination into the same reservoirs, and utilizing existing techniques for color noise and disocclusion noise reduction.

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting is a popular representation for radiance field reconstruction, distinguished by the rendering speed of its rasterization-based renderer. While 3D Gaussians can also be raytraced, this approach has so far been slower, with 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing (3DGRT) taking nearly one order of magnitude longer to optimize. To address this, we present GRay, a fast ray tracer for 3D Gaussians designed to close this performance gap and match 3DGS's speed. Our method leverages the algorithmic difference between both approaches: unlike rasterization, ray tracing evaluates only Gaussians that are actually intersected by a ray, leading to potentially logarithmic—rather than linear—scaling in the number of primitives. This property allows ray tracing to better exploit dense scenes composed of numerous tiny Gaussians, a configuration which has largely been overlooked. Notably, we show that dense initialization—which creates many small primitives—slows down rasterization, but instead speeds up ray tracing. Designed to leverage this effect, GRay renders nearly 4× faster and optimizes nearly 10× faster than 3DGRT while maintaining similar quality, and has competitive speed with 3DGS albeit with somewhat lower quality. Code will be released upon publication.

abstract: Implicit surfaces offer distinct advantages over traditional boundary representations, including infinite resolution, low memory footprint, smooth geometry by construction, and support for non-destructive modeling. In this work, we introduce a method for localizing geometric detail in a way that preserves the mathematical properties required for accurate and efficient rendering using sphere tracing. Our contributions include novel procedural modeling techniques that expand the range of repetition patterns achievable in implicit surfaces; an interpolation-based approach that maintains field correctness while remaining computationally efficient; and a cache-based acceleration strategy that significantly improves the rendering performance of domain-repeated implicit geometries.

abstract: Frametime spikes and graphical fidelity both influence the feel of first-person shooter (FPS) games, yet their combined effects are not well understood. This paper examines how graphics settings and frametime spike magnitude interact with player performance and experience. We developed a custom FPS game with configurable textures, lighting, and visual effects, and induced frametime spikes of 0~ms, 225~ms, or 675~ms during play. Twenty-one participants completed all combinations while providing performance data and subjective ratings for visual quality and smoothness. Results show that graphical fidelity primarily affects perceived visual quality, while frametime spikes strongly reduce perceived smoothness. Performance (i.e., score and accuracy) declines with larger spikes but remains largely unchanged across graphics settings. These findings suggest that spike magnitude, rather than graphical fidelity, is the dominant factor shaping smoothness and performance, while players still notice and prefer higher-fidelity visuals.

abstract: In this paper, we rethink the controllable motion synthesis as a problem of manifold restriction rather than manifold construction. Based on this perspective, we propose a prior-first, condition-second framework for body-conditioned hand motion completion. Our framework first learns a generic body–hand kinematic prior from large-scale unstructured and unlabeled motion data, capturing the intrinsic coordination between global body dynamics and hand articulation. Semantic control is then introduced through lightweight adaptation on top of the frozen prior, avoiding the need to relearn kinematic structure for each control interface. At the core of our framework is a streaming, autoregressive body–hand prior that completes temporally coherent and kinematically consistent hand motion given global body motion. The prior is designed for online inference and real-time use, and incorporates structured kinematic modeling to maintain mechanical coupling between the body and the hands. To enable practical controllability under limited supervision, we introduce semantically-layered adapters that inject conditioning signals at appropriate kinematic levels, supporting both self-supervised attribute control and weakly supervised text-driven control with only a few hours of labeled data. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our framework improves kinematic plausibility, robustness, and controllability compared to end-to-end conditioned baselines, particularly in low-resource and cross-dataset settings. We further showcase real-time inference and an interactive authoring workflow, highlighting the applicability to production animation pipelines.

abstract: In computer graphics and engineering, isotropic hyperelastic volumetric materials are commonly chosen from a small set of families (e.g., StVK, linear corotational, Neo-Hookean, Ogden) and tuned by adjusting family-specific parameters. This workflow obscures how different material families relate and provides no unified notion of “distance” or “amount and direction of nonlinearity” across families. Furthermore, for a general isotropic 3D hyperelastic energy density function y; the relationships between its parameter values, and visually intuitive properties such as an object’s “stiffness”, volume preservation, or the “amount of nonlinearity”, are less clear and can be tedious to adjust. Starting with an arbitrary isotropic y; we define and compute Lamé parameters (capturing linear behavior: stiffness and volume preservation), using the Taylor expansion of y at the rest state. This makes it possible to quantitatively “equalize” the small-deformation behavior of two materials, even if they come from different material families, or are defined by arbitrary isotropic energy densities y: We rigorously state and prove that Linear Corotational materials (arguably the most widely used materials in computer graphics) are the simplest possible nonlinear materials. To compare nonlinear behavior beyond the linearization, we define a distance metric between linearization-matched materials, using third-order terms of y (“weakly nonlinear behavior”). We further define SCIEN, a directional nonlinearity measure obtained by projecting a material onto the standard one-parameter Seth-Hill continuum (which includes Hencky, Linear Corotational, and StVK as special cases), thereby distinguishing stretch-stiffening from compressionstiffening and quantifying its strength. As a result, we can equalize and edit materials agnostically from any material family: two materials can be matched in small-deformation response, in weakly nonlinear behavior, or in both, while keeping these properties decoupled. abstract: Music-driven character animation enables and enhances transformative applications in entertainment and interactive education. However, synthesizing realistic drumming motion from audio remains challenging due to the inherent tension between high-acceleration dynamics and the need for extreme spatial-temporal precision. Existing approaches, often reliant on motion matching or MIDI input, struggle with generalizing to diverse real-world audio. Moreover, the field lacks standardized evaluation metrics capable of distinguishing precise drumming from noisy motion. In this paper, we introduce a generative diffusion framework featuring a dual-objective loss function that decouples skeletal integrity from drumstick precision, thus enabling centimeter-level stick precision without sacrificing natural body dynamics. Additionally, leveraging our own dataset and data augmentation strategy, the model generalizes to non-curated, in-the-wild audio. To rigorously evaluate performance, we propose two novel metrics: an impact-to-target distance to quantify spatial precision and an audio-motion correlation score to assess temporal alignment. Our quantitative analysis and user studies demonstrate that our system generates high-quality motion that is often indistinguishable from ground-truth performances.

abstract: Reconstructions of surgical scenes from endoscopic video are useful for surgical training and medical animation, as they accurately capture the clinician’s viewpoint. In practice, however, 3D scenes acquired through endoscopy, increasingly represented as 3D Gaussian splats (3DGS), are typically constrained to limited viewpoint ranges. Consequently, even small endoscope camera motions can significantly degrade rendering fidelity and organ shape reconstruction. This gap prevents the direct use of such scenes in physics-based surgical simulation, which requires accurate, shape-consistent geometry. To address this, we propose a pipeline that combines the visual realism of an endoscopic 3DGS scene with simulation-ready organ geometry extracted from pre-operative 3D computed tomography (CT) or MRI scans. Because the pre-operative and endoscopically observed organs often differ in pose, deformation, and geometric completeness, we register the full segmented anatomy onto its partial corresponding region in the splat representation using a mesh-free, elastically regularized alignment method. We perform this alignment in the reduced-order deformation space of Simplicits, an existing state-of-the-art mesh-free simulator based on learned skinning weights, which has not previously been applied to surgical endoscope-captured organs because no CT-grounded alignment pipeline existed to bridge the two modalities. Using its reduced basis, we optimize on the order of 10–20 handle transforms rather than thousands of tetrahedral-mesh vertices. We employ a two-stage procedure: (1) a weighted rigid iterative closest point (ICP), (2) followed by a reduced-order elastic ICP, with a Neo-Hookean elastic energy term and a geometry matching term that uses nearest-neighbour correspondences to the 3DGS target. As shown in Figure 1, our pipeline produces CT-grounded, physics-simulatable organ assets that are visually aligned with the hyper-realistic tissue surfaces captured by endoscopic 3DGS reconstructions, closing the gap between photoreal scene capture and simulation-ready geometry.

abstract: Traditional garment simulation for animated characters is a time-consuming bottleneck for artists due to slow simulations and tedious parameter tunings. Recent data-driven methods offer a powerful alternative, capable of learning from a dataset of simulated data to generate high-quality deformations. A lightweight network design allows data-driven systems to achieve a real-time inference speed. This significantly improves the artist workflow, as they can interactively pose a character and see high-quality folds and wrinkles at animation time, thereby allowing to make creative decisions ahead of time. However, existing neural clothing methods have presented appealing results on datasets based on realistic human models (e.g., SMPL), but when trained on animated character datasets, they struggle to generalize to unseen poses. In this paper, we aim at designing neural networks and training strategies to generalize better to unseen poses in real-time to enable the interactive posing applications. We focus on a production-oriented setting where the model is trained for a single garment in a quasi-static setup. Technically, we leverage a smooth, expressive latent space by first training a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). We then progressively train the VAE encoder to transition from reconstruction to pose-driven prediction. To guide this prediction, we condition the network on both low-dimensional pose parameters and character body surface displacements. Finally, we introduce a novel local gradient histogram loss that mitigates the over-smoothing effect of reconstruction losses. Extensive evaluations on production-level assets and public datasets demonstrate that our method produces sharp, realistic wrinkles, smooth large-scale drape, and temporal coherence in real-time, offering a robust and easily integrable solution for interactive posing workflows.

abstract: Speech-driven 3D facial animation plays a pivotal role in immersive digital human applications. Recent works have explored Mamba-based sequence modeling as an efficient alternative to Transformer, but they often suffer from limited cross-modal alignment and insufficient control over fine-grained facial deformations. To address these limitations, we propose FaceMamba framework. First, we introduce a Multi-Granularity Audio Encoder (MG-AE) to provide richer conditioning for motion synthesis. Second, we propose a Gated-Cross Mamba Decoder (GC-MD), which performs dynamic modulation of audio features within the state-space modeling process, significantly improving audio-visual alignment while retaining near-linear complexity. We further design a 3D structural consistency loss (Lstruct ) that explicitly enforces anatomically plausible facial deformations in mesh space. In addition, we introduce a geometry-aware evaluation metric to quantitatively assess the structural fidelity of generated 3D facial sequences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FaceMamba outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving the MVE and ESE metrics by 2.3% and 2.9% on BIWI, and by 2.8% and 4.0% on Vocaset, respectively. Notably, for a 20-second sequence, our framework keeps the inference time under 0.25s, which is 1.6x faster than the SOTA. Our work provides new insights into geometry-aware audio-driven facial synthesis.

abstract: Garment animation systems are essential for high-fidelity digital characters in various applications such as films and video games. We propose SSILK, a neural network-based method that is explicitly designed to handle loose garments such as capes and robes, garment types that are notoriously hard to simulate via pose-based garment neural simulators. We achieve this through three contributions. First, we formulate our method as a latent-space time integration scheme inspired by Verlet integration, resulting in more temporally stable garment dynamics compared to prior methods. Second, we employ a hybrid proxy-joint and blendshape decoder to represent full SO(3) transformations that can be too challenging to capture using blendshapes alone. Finally, we propose a data-augmentation strategy to improve performance on out-of-distribution scenarios. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on various garment and character animations and compare it to the state of the art.

abstract: Realistic animal motion for virtual production is typically obtained either through motion capture of highly trained performers who accurately mimic animal behavior, or by retargeting ordinary human motion using complex control setups. Both approaches are challenging and often fail to fully reproduce the nuances of natural animal motion, motivating data-driven alternatives. We present an automatic human-to-quadruped puppeteering framework that produces plausible and controllable quadruped motions from ordinary human motion data. Our approach employs a two-stage generative diffusion model trained purely on quadruped motion data. By introducing a structured conditioning and inpainting strategy, our method supports a wide range of actions, including walking, running, jumping, sitting, and lying. Furthermore, we enable fine-grained intuitive control of the quadruped motion such as head movement control and individual limb puppeteering. Experimental results demonstrate improved motion realism and controllability compared to existing retargeting approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of our framework as a tool for animation and virtual production applications.

abstract: Motion editing is central to VFX and game development, where it is used extensively to modify and augment existing movements to conform to new environments or changes in artistic direction. While traditional motion editing can do small modifications, it cannot accommodate larger structural edits, resulting in visual warping artifacts that require authoring new motion. Conversely, recent advances in large-scale generative modeling have unlocked newfound capabilities for authoring entire movements by directly manipulating sparse spatial constraints. While impressive at creating new movements, these methods lack the capability to preserve and edit existing motion interactively. In this work, we introduce scheduled inpainting, a method that enables interactive generative motion editing, a novel paradigm unifying motion synthesis and editing by leveraging generative models. Scheduled inpainting is a simple yet powerful inference-based technique that enables fine-grained spatiotemporal control over the balance between preserving the original motion and generating new content. By building atop generative models that support direct manipulation, our system allows artists to interactively refine existing animations while ensuring results remain natural and consistent with the learned motion distribution. Scheduled inpainting is versatile and supports many editing applications, such as extending, stitching, and compositing different clips. Finally, we extensively validate our approach by comparing with four baselines, conducting ablations of our design, and reporting user feedback.

abstract: Speech-driven 3D facial animation has achieved remarkable realism, yet existing models suffer from severe performance degradation on unseen languages due to discrepancies in articulation patterns and motion distributions. We attribute this limitation to a distribution shift on the latent motion manifold, where pretrained vector-quantized (VQ) codebooks fail to adequately cover target-language articulation regions. To address this, we propose Manifold-Aligned VQ Convolutional Adapters for parameter-efficient cross-lingual adaptation. Instead of retraining the entire backbone, we insert lightweight 1D convolutional adapters into the post-quantization and decoder stages, formulating adaptation as a localized geometric correction on the motion manifold. Theoretically, we demonstrate that under the local bi-Lipschitz continuity of the pretrained decoder, minimizing reconstruction loss effectively aligns the latent motion distribution with the target language. Unlike conventional linear adapters, our convolutional design explicitly captures local temporal dependencies and higher-order motion dynamics critical for language-specific articulation. To support systematic evaluation, we construct CMLR-3D, a paired Mandarin speech–3D facial motion dataset. Extensive experiments on CodeTalker and ARTalk show that our method significantly improves lip synchronization and motion naturalness, consistently outperforming full and partial fine-tuning baselines in both quantitative metrics (LVE, AVLR) and perceptual user studies. Notably, the framework updates only 0.46%–1.26% of parameters while preserving pretrained motion priors. This work provides a theoretically grounded, highly efficient paradigm for multilingual virtual avatar deployment. (Anonymous link http:github.com/GreenTomato-hugo/MAVQ-Adapter)

abstract: Abstract Motivation Aquatic duckweeds, including Wolffia australiana, are the smallest and fastest growing flowering plants on the planet, with numerous emerging biotechnological applications. Duckweed populations grow through rapid clonal budding, but existing phenotypic characterization and image analysis tools typically operate only at the population level, tracking neither individual plants nor their lineage structure. Deepweed addresses this gap, combining automated individual segmentation, temporal tracking, and clonal lineage reconstruction from time-lapse imaging of duckweed. Results Deepweed processes time-lapse duckweed imaging datasets using deep-learning–based instance segmentation and multi-object tracking to assign persistent identities to individual fronds and infer mother–daughter relationships. The workflow outputs lineage graphs, individual-level morphological metrics, and population-level growth summaries, supported by lineage-annotated time-lapse visualizations. Applied to dense Wolffia populations, in both freely growing or controlled microfluidic environments, our framework can track hundreds of Wolffia plants simultaneously, resolves overlapping individuals, and reconstructs multi-generation lineage structure, enabling analyses that are inaccessible with population-level phenotyping methods. Availability Deepweed is implemented in Python using PyTorch, scikit-image, OpenCV, and btrack. Source code, trained models, example datasets, and documentation are freely available at https://github.com/SamOliveiraLab/Deepweed. The Deepweed code is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18844282 and the datasets are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18843917. abstract: Abstract Motivation Ancient DNA (aDNA) research has advanced rapidly with the development of high-throughput sequencing, enabling genome-wide analyses of large collections of prehistoric specimens. However, analysing palaeontological and archaeological material with highly degraded DNA constitutes a major bioinformatic challenge. DNA from such samples is characterized by short fragment lengths, low endogenous content, post-mortem damage, and cross-species contamination, which can increase spurious mapping and reference bias, affecting downstream population genetic inferences. Results We present DNAharvester, a modular and reproducible pipeline designed specifically for processing highly degraded DNA from ancient and historical specimens. DNAharvester integrates metagenomic filtering, competitive mapping, adaptive aligner selection (incorporating BWA-aln, BWA-mem, and Bowtie2), and systematic evaluation of reference bias and spurious mapping. By incorporating flexible mapping and filtering strategies, the pipeline can be adapted to varying sample preservation, focusing on maximizing authentic data recovery. DNAharvester features subworkflows for iterative assembly of mitogenomes, identification of genomic repeats and CpG sites, taxonomic classification, microbial/pathogen screening, genetic sex determination, and variant calling. To accommodate varying sequencing depths, the pipeline supports diploid variant calling, genotype likelihood estimation, and pseudo-haploid random allele calling. We validated the pipeline using simulated and empirical datasets, demonstrating its ability to systematically mitigate complex background contamination while preserving authentic genomic signals. By streamlining complex bioinformatic tasks through simple configuration files, DNAharvester establishes a standardized approach for analysing aDNA datasets and makes genomic analyses of ancient remains accessible to the broader research community. Availability and Implementation Implemented in Nextflow, DNAharvester provides a highly scalable, containerized framework that enhances reproducibility, portability, and robustness in aDNA analyses. DNAharvester is open source under the GNU General Public License v3.0 and freely available at https://github.com/NBISweden/DNAharvester. abstract: Abstract Motivation Protein-ligand binding site prediction (LBS) is important for many areas of structural biology and molecular modeling, where, as in other tasks, protein language models (pLMs) have shown great promise. In their application to LBS, the pLM classifies each amino acid as binding or not, but translating these predictions into three-dimensional binding pockets remains challenging; in particular, residue-centric predictions tend to produce spatially fragmented pockets. Results We present Seq2Pocket, a methodology for pocket-level LBS prediction that combines pLM finetuning, data enhancement, and structure-aware post-processing. First, we introduce sc-PDBenhanced, an extended training dataset that augments an existing sc-PDB dataset with additional small-molecule and ion-binding sites, improving coverage of non-obvious and small pockets. Second, we employ an embedding-supported smoothing classifier to refine residue-level predictions. Third, we define the Pocket Fragmentation Index and use it to select a clustering approach that preserves a consistent mapping between predictions and ground-truth pockets. We evaluate Seq2Pocket on two tasks: general binding site prediction using the LIGYSIS benchmark and cryptic binding site prediction using CryptoBench benchmark. Across both benchmarks, Seq2Pocket achieves state-of-the-art DCCtop-N and DCCtop-(N+2) performance. In particular, for general binding site prediction on the LIGYSIS benchmark, it improves distance-center-to-center recall by up to 13%, outperforming existing predictors. This improvement originates from training data quality rather than model architecture, as demonstrated by an ablation study. We believe that these findings contribute to more reliable evaluation practices in ligand binding site prediction, highlight the importance of training data curation, and provide pocket-level prediction tools that are better suited for downstream applications such as drug discovery. Availability The Seq2Pocket web interface is available at https://seq2pocket.projekty.ms.mff.cuni.cz, running the ESM-2 650M variant. The sc-PDBenhanced is published using Zenodo platform at https://zenodo.org/records/18271517 [Škrhák and Hoksza 2026]. abstract: Abstract Motivation Understanding disease-related causal mechanisms is essential for biomedical research, yet the practical use of Mendelian Randomization (MR) remains constrained by fragmented analytical workflows and a strong dependence on specialized expertise. These challenges limit the efficient, standardized, and reproducible execution of end-to-end MR analyses. Results We propose MR-MAS, an end-to-end automated MR analysis system built on a multi-agent architecture. MR-MAS leverages the reasoning and coordination capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and integrates external tools to unify data acquisition, causal effect estimation, results interpretation, and manuscript preparation into a single workflow, thereby reducing manual effort. MR-MAS further incorporates a structured Mendelian Randomization Knowledge Base (MRKB) to support MR method implementation and targeted repair of MR analysis code. Across diverse test scenarios, MR-MAS demonstrated stable workflow execution, reproduced several literature-supported causal signals, and maintained consistent causal estimates across repeated runs and different model backends. Additional evaluations showed robust trait retrieval and improved code-repair performance with MRKB guidance. These results suggest that MR-MAS may provide practical support for scalable, standardized, and reproducible MR analyses in biomedical research. Availability and Implementation The source code, MRKB, and benchmark data are freely available at https://github.com/Zaiwen/MR-MAS, with the version used in this study archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20342636.

abstract: Abstract Motivation Automated cytology screening is essential for early cervical cancer prevention, where gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs) are typically partitioned into tiles for tile-level feature extraction and subsequent WSI-level diagnosis aggregation. However, existing tile-level methods remain constrained by limited input sizes, which frequently obscures sparse and morphologically subtle abnormal cells. Furthermore, these methods commonly formulate tile-level representation learning as a coarse single-label classification task, thereby failing to capture the complex co-occurrence patterns and morphological heterogeneity of cervical cytological abnormalities. Results We propose the Frequency-Aware Multi-Label Learning Network (FMCerNet), a tile-level feature extractor equipped with a Large-Field Frequency-Enhanced ViT (LFreq-ViT) backbone and a Coarse-to-Fine multi-label classification (C2F) head. The former incorporates a Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform module to efficiently extract frequency-domain features from large-scale tiles, whereas the latter enhances fine-grained tile representation decoding through hierarchical supervision. Experiments on both public and private datasets demonstrate that FMCerNet improves the accuracy of positive screening and fine-grained subtype classification while maintaining high inference speed. abstract: Abstract Summary Linkage disequilibrium (LD) information from one’s own dataset is considered optimal for downstream analyses such as statistical fine-mapping. However, the computational complexity (≈N22 computations for N variants) lead most studies to use external reference panels, such as from 1000 Genomes. To capture LD across all variant pairs in biobank-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) datasets with hundreds of millions of variants, new computational strategies are essential. We present a novel approach that uses multi-GPU distributed computing to compute R2 for every variant pair in a dataset. On chromosome 22 (1.8 million variants) of the 30x WGS 1000 Genomes dataset, our method using eight consumer-level 12GB GPUs (NVIDIA RTX 2080TIs) takes <10 minutes, while the same calculation with PLINK using a high-end 64-threaded CPU (Intel Xeon Gold 6338) takes > 80 minutes, corresponding to a ≈8x speedup. We further demonstrate true biobank-scale performance in the Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; 57,170 samples), computing chromosome 1 LD (≈1.38 million variants) in 49 minutes versus 22.7 hours for PLINK, a ≈28x speedup. With this method, we successfully computed on the aforementioned 30x WGS 1000 Genomes dataset (≈120 million variants and ≈2500 samples) the entire LD matrix ($>$1e16, or 10 quadrillion elements) in under 6 hours using 512 NVIDIA 40GB A100 GPUs on the Department of Energy Argonne Leadership Computing Facility Polaris Supercomputer. We make this tool, coded in Python using CuPy, publicly available. Using this tool, researchers can leverage the full extent of their genomic data without relying on external LD reference panels and acquire more accurate, population-specific findings, particularly for groups underrepresented in existing databases. Availability and Implementation ARCHER-LD is an open-source tool available on GitHub under the Apache License 2.0 at https://github.com/rachitk/ARCHER-LD. abstract: Abstract Motivation Designing regulatory DNA sequences is challenging due to their discrete nucleotide alphabet and complex higher-order dependencies underlying regulatory function. Many existing generative models, particularly diffusion-based approaches, learn by injecting stochastic noise into sequences and training denoising processes, which can distort discrete sequence structure and weaken biological constraints. Results Here, we introduce DNA Bayesian Flow Networks (DNA-BFN), a generative framework that models regulatory DNA sequences through iterative Bayesian updates of per-position nucleotide distributions. By directly modeling per-position categorical beliefs, DNA-BFN realizes a diffusion-like generative process without explicitly perturbing discrete nucleotide sequences, enabling fully differentiable training while preserving discrete sequence structure. Across eight regulatory sequence datasets spanning diverse species, scales, and sequence lengths, DNA-BFN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, faithfully preserves sequence feature statistics and regulatory patterns, enables few-shot sequence design, and achieves faster sampling efficiency. These results show that framing sequence generation as progressive uncertainty reduction in probability space provides an effective and generalizable approach for nucleotide sequence design. Availability The software and its source code are publicly available at https://github.com/WangLabTHU/DNA-BFN. abstract: Abstract Motivation The rising incidence of antifungal drug resistance represents a major and growing threat to global public health and food security. Therefore, understanding the genetic and molecular mechanisms that underpin antifungal resistance is essential for both clinical management and agricultural disease control. Results We present MARDy 2.0, an updated platform replacing the original Mycology Antifungal Resistance Database. MARDy 2.0 provides an interactive platform for exploring antifungal resistance data from the community resource FungAMR, and protein structures from UniProtKB or predicted structures using AlphaFold. The platform provides enhanced tools for data exploration and analysis and is freely accessible via an interactive web interface that supports search filtering and downloads, BLAST-based sequence similarity searches, an experimental natural-language query interface for exploratory analysis, a mutation plot for visualising mutations in a protein context, and structural predictions showing mutation locations. MARDy 2.0 provides a platform to facilitate research into antifungal resistance evolution, surveillance, and mitigation strategies. MARDy should be used and cited alongside the underlying resources it integrates, FungAMR. Availability Accessible at https://mardy.net

abstract: Abstract Motivation Although large scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many risk variants for psychiatric traits their functional implication remain largely unknown. One potential mechanism for their risk is through cellular context-dependent epigenetics such as methylation. Previous methodologies have focused on integrating GWAS with single cell transcriptomics, which allowed identification of within-cell-type heterogeneity in disease risk association. We extended this framework to provide a method called met-scDRS that integrates GWAS with single cell epigenomics and investigates how psychiatric disease risk can manifest through methylomics at single cell resolution. Results We propose an approach that integrates single cell methylomes with disease associated genes identified from GWAS at single-cell resolution. We found our method to be well calibrated and powered in different scenarios. We then analyzed a publicly available single cell methylome dataset of the human brain for 75 different traits and generated disease relevance scores for each cell for each trait. We find high brain specificity with major cell type enrichments congruent with known findings. We identify within-cell-type heterogeneity for psychiatric disease risk along the brain spatial axis as well as subpopulations that are differentially associated with diseases. Finally, we showed that genes with high correlation between methylation levels and disease relevance scores to be highly enriched in specific functional pathways such as synaptic formation and transmission. Availability met-scDRS is freely available in GitHub as a python package under MIT license: https://github.com/bogdanlab/met-scDRS. Source code is also available from Zenodo with DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21841506. All dataset used in this work are publicly available. abstract: Abstract Motivation Differential gene expression (DGE) analysis is foundational for interpreting RNA sequencing data, but it conflates direct biological effects with correlations propagated through gene co-expression. Across three RNA sequencing datasets (including a genome-scale perturb-seq experiment), we find that only a small fraction of differentially expressed genes have direct effects on the trait of interest, while the majority are undirected or passengers whose associations are mediated through other genes. Results To distinguish direct effect genes, we introduce conditional differential gene expression (CDGE) analysis, a framework that tests for conditional rather than marginal association between each gene and the trait of interest. Implemented via the GhostKnockoff procedure with lasso regression, CDGE delivers false discovery rate control, operates on summary statistics from existing DGE pipelines, and accommodates batch effects. The genes identified by CDGE mediate the effects of most other differentially expressed genes and show stronger enrichment for known protein-protein interactions and biological pathways than DGE-identified genes. These results suggest that the field has been systematically over-interpreting DGE outputs, and that distinguishing direct from mediated effects is essential for prioritizing genes for functional follow-up and therapeutic development. Availability To facilitate public access to knockoff-based CDGE analysis, we have developed the R package “KnockoffCDGE” as an integrated implementation, which is freely available at https://github.com/GuJQ5/KnockoffCDGE (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23241517). Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

abstract: Abstract Summary Human genetic evidence provides a strong foundation for selecting drug targets. However, consistent benchmarking of target-indication evidence against clinical trial outcomes has been hindered by proprietary data and customised pipelines. To address this, we present the Python package ct-validation, which evaluates whether target-indication pairs supported by specific evidence sources are enriched for clinical progression. This package computes relative success (RS) and odds ratios (OR) with confidence intervals across clinical phase transitions. It also supports ontology-based semantic disease matching and offers interfaces in Python, on the command line, and via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). By remapping the benchmark from Minikel et al. (2024) to the Experimental Factor Ontology (EFO), we reproduced their per-transition enrichment, with a maximum difference of only 1.4% across any transition. In a systematic 3x3 benchmark that independently varies the genetic evidence and clinical trial sources, we found that a single curated open clinical trial source reproduces the signal of the proprietary comparator (RS = 2.92 vs 2.65; 2.34 vs 2.55 without oncology). However, aggregating open clinical trial registries compresses this signal (RS = 1.52); this loss is primarily driven by the breadth of the indication data rather than the genetic evidence. Availability and implementation ct-validation is implemented in Python (version 3.11 or higher), distributed via pip, and freely available at https://github.com/gero-science/ct-validation, with support for Python, command-line, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) interfaces. Archived code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22901497. Benchmark data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22901451. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

abstract: Abstract Virtual cells aim to represent cellular states computationally and predict responses to genetic, chemical, environmental, temporal, and spatial conditions. For comparative purposes, this review uses state encoding (E), state transition (T), and observation decoding (D) as a conceptual abstraction spanning explicit mechanistic models, data-driven foundation and perturbation models, multimodal systems, and spatial and multiscale simulation. We examine model boundaries, data foundations, resource disclosure, out-of-distribution evaluation, causal evidence, and experimental validation. Independent benchmarks show that parameter count and training-set size do not automatically yield robust out-of-distribution generalization, while transcriptomic representations alone do not capture the full functional state of a cell. Trustworthy virtual cells will require perturbation-responsive transitions, cross-modal alignment, continuous-time dynamics, mechanistic constraints, calibrated uncertainty, independent experimental validation, and, where appropriate, closed-loop experimental feedback.

abstract: Abstract Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells and invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells are conventionally identified using invariant or semi-invariant TCRα chains, antigen-loaded tetramers, or transcriptomic phenotypes. These requirements limit their detection in public and clinical immune-repertoire datasets that contain only TCRβ sequences. Here we present UcTCRp, a TCRβ-only framework for detecting and profiling relative MAIT- and iNKT-associated signals in bulk immune repertoires. We first identified model-informative TCRβ features, including biased V-gene usage and reproducible CDR3β amino acid composition, in collected human and mouse MAIT and iNKT TCRβ sequences. UcTCRp subsequently integrates these features using species-specific transformer-based representation pretrained separately on large human and mouse TCRβ repertoires, followed by independent supervised modeling with curated MAIT, iNKT, and conventional T cell references for each species. The resulting species-specific models generalized robustly across independent human and mouse cohorts. In paired scRNA-seq/scTCR-seq datasets, UcTCRp recovered transcriptome-defined MAIT and iNKT cells and identified additional MAIT-like candidates supported by receptor evidence but missed by expression-only annotation. Bulk calibration against paired single-cell references and synthetic spike-in experiments established operating characteristics for repertoire-level abundance estimation. These results establish unpaired TCRβ repertoires as an actionable substrate for detecting relative unconventional T cell-associated immune signals, enabling archived repertoire resources to be repurposed for systems-level studies of tissue immunity, disease, and therapeutic response.

abstract: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics (STs) measures gene expression while retaining the location of transcripts or cells within tissue sections. Unlike bulk RNA sequencing, which averages expression across cell populations, and single-cell RNA sequencing, which generally requires tissue dissociation, ST links molecular profiles to tissue architecture. This spatial information supports the analysis of tissue heterogeneity, cellular organization, and potential intercellular interactions. The spatially resolved nature of ST has unlocked diverse applications in fields such as cancer, neuroscience, reproductive biology, and plant biology. In parallel, the development of publicly accessible databases and repositories has facilitated large-scale, multi-cohort comparisons and benchmarking. The rapid expansion and increasing complexity of these datasets have driven the adoption of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques. These computational tools support a range of tasks, including data pre-processing, image segmentation, spatial domain identification, and pattern recognition. Moreover, they are instrumental in integrative multi-omics analyses and predictive modeling. This AI-focused review provides necessary background on ST technologies and databases and evaluates the use of statistical, ML, and DL methods across the analytical workflow, from image and sequencing-data preprocessing to spatial analysis and LLM-assisted interpretation. We compile key resources related to datasets, AI-driven analytical frameworks, and ST data analysis pipelines, and discuss current challenges, limitations, and future directions for AI-based tools in spatial omics.

abstract: Abstract The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and bioinformatics is reshaping the landscape of precision medicine in brain diseases, particularly in neurological diseases and brain tumors. Despite advances in both fields, the combined application of radiomics and multi-omics fusion remains underutilized, even though integrative frameworks are essential for addressing the complexity and heterogeneity of imaging and molecular data. This review examines how integrative AI-bioinformatics frameworks enable the fusion of radiomics with genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and other omics modalities to more comprehensively model disease complexity. Leveraging deep learning, graph neural networks, and advanced representation learning, these multimodal systems facilitate biomarker discovery, patient stratification, and personalized treatment strategies. We critically evaluate key challenges including data heterogeneity, limited interpretability, and barriers to clinical validation, and highlight emerging solutions aimed at enhancing reproducibility and translational readiness. Case studies in gliomas, Alzheimer’s disease, and multiple sclerosis illustrate the clinical utility of unified imaging-omics architectures. Ultimately, this review positions radiomics and multi-omics integration as a foundational approach for the next generation of precision medicine in brain diseases by bridging the gap between computational innovation and clinical application.

abstract: Abstract Ribosome heterogeneity is increasingly recognized as a key factor in various biological contexts, including development, cancer, and immune responses. To enable systematic exploration of this diversity, we previously developed a bioinformatics method that utilized rRNA reads from Ribo-seq data, detecting changes in ribosomal protein composition (dripARF) and ribosome collisions (dricARF) between conditions simply and efficiently. The method works by projecting differences in rRNA read abundance onto the 3D-structure of the ribosome, following which we perform enrichment tests on predefined heterogeneity-specific rRNA position sets. In this study, we apply this tool to publicly available Ribo-seq datasets to understand the impact of experimental protocol variations and to identify shared biological signals across studies. Our analyses show that the rRNA regions assigned to our prediction sets are consistently enriched in rRNA reads, supporting the core assumptions of our approach. We further examine how various protocol factors influence rRNA read distribution and implement a single-sample rRNA position set enrichment analysis-based weight to limit false positives. Finally, we highlight consistent ribosomal changes across these studies, including prominent co-predictors such as ribosome collisions, eS25, and uS19.

abstract: Abstract Disease progression is driven not only by transcriptional alterations but also by dynamic reorganization of molecular interaction networks. However, most existing approaches focus on differential gene expression and fail to capture modular-level reorganization. Here, we present dynamic perturbation analysis (DPA), a modular rewiring framework that quantifies dynamic perturbations across disease stages using a novel metric termed the degree of perturbation. Using gastric cancer (GC) progression as a model system, DPA revealed that extensive modular rewiring persists despite limited stage-specific transcriptional changes after tumor initiation. DPA identified progression-associated perturbation programs characterized by extracellular matrix remodeling, oncogenic signaling activation, stemness acquisition, and late-stage microenvironmental adaptation. Perturbation analysis revealed two major disease-driving programs and prioritized previously unrecognized regulators, including protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 12 (PTPN12) and leucine rich repeat and Ig domain containing 1 (LINGO1), whose functional roles in GC progression were experimentally validated. Furthermore, modular rewiring-guided drug repurposing uncovered PJ-34 as a promising therapeutic candidate targeting late-stage disease-associated perturbations. Collectively, DPA provides a generalizable framework for decoding disease progression through dynamic modular rewiring, enabling the identification of driver programs, candidate regulators, and therapeutic vulnerabilities. This framework offers a scalable strategy for network-guided mechanistic discovery and therapeutic prioritization in complex diseases.

abstract: Abstract Public repositories now accumulate an unprecedented amount of metabolomics data. Despite the opportunities for large-scale meta-analyses opened by these repositories, the deposited data rarely becomes systematically re-analyzed. We conducted a systematic metadata-based re-analysis of all human blood metabolomics studies in the Metabolomics Workbench performed using Orbitrap or QTOF mass spectrometry, encompassing 44 165 samples. After harmonizing metabolites with PubChem identifiers and embedding them using SMILES representations, we generated a map of 6752 blood metabolites forming 25 structural clusters, and subsequently performed correlation analysis between these clusters, biomarkers, and drugs. Analysis of 337 120 metabolite pairs detected in at least 10 studies showed that structurally related clusters display correlated abundances (ρ up to 0.6). Correlation patterns among established clinical biomarkers revealed candidate metabolic correlates, several with ρ > 0.7. We also developed open-source software enabling similar analyses for any metabolite across the Workbench data explored. Additionally, curating drug-containing datasets enabled meta-analyses for compounds such as acetaminophen, metoprolol, and atenolol, identifying both known and novel metabolic signatures. Besides the biological insights, we have found that Orbitrap and QTOF tend to detect different metabolites, but they give quantitatively coherent results on overlapping compounds. Overall, the present study provides the methodology and software to perform large-scale mining of public metabolomics data enabling its re-analysis to obtain novel biomedical insights.

abstract: Abstract Drug metabolism by gut microorganisms is bacteria-specific and can have clinically significant consequences, including prodrug activation, drug inactivation, and the generation of toxic metabolites. However, existing computational approaches have primarily focused on community-level predictions or drug-to-microbe effects, without resolving the metabolic contributions of individual bacterial strains or the bidirectional nature of drug–bacteria interactions, despite advances in computational frameworks. Here, we propose a bidirectional cross-attention architecture, multimodal Bi-MHA, that integrates atom-level molecular embeddings and protein-level bacterial embeddings from pretrained models to generate a combined representation for classification. The proposed model was developed using reliability stratification and a $\mathrm{\lambda}$-scaled loss function on the training dataset and achieved consistent performance across three unseen tasks: unseen drug (receiver operating characteristic area under the curve [ROC AUC]: 0.690), unseen bacteria (ROC AUC: 0.920), and unseen interaction (ROC AUC: 0.949), ranking first among all compared models in the rank-sum metric. Beyond prediction, attention-based analysis not only indicated enzymatic reaction sites that were experimentally validated in previous studies but also prioritized candidate bacterial proteins, demonstrating interpretability at both the atom and protein levels. The proposed model also achieved a 15 percentage point improvement in accuracy over the KNN baseline on an external validation dataset of 85 out-of-distribution drug-bacteria pairs. Furthermore, the model was extended to community-level prediction as a proof-of-concept application using a weighted-abundance pipeline on an independent microbiome dataset. These results demonstrate the model’s potential as an interpretable screening tool for drug safety evaluation and personalized medicine. The source code is available at https://github.com/Jaehyeon-O-Ob/Bacteria-Specific_Drug_Metabolism.

abstract: Abstract Increasingly diverse, multi-ancestry genome-wide association studies (GWASs) provide unprecedented opportunities to better understand the genetic architecture of complex traits. In particular, differences in linkage disequilibrium (LD) patterns across populations can be leveraged to improve the resolution and reliability of statistical fine-mapping. However, cross-ancestry effect heterogeneity, population-specific variant support, and LD mismatches pose substantial challenges, motivating a systematic evaluation of multi-ancestry fine-mapping methods to provide practical guidance for analyses across diverse populations. We conducted a comprehensive benchmarking of nine methods, spanning joint probabilistic models that explicitly model cross-ancestry LD and effect sharing, and univariate-based integration approaches that aggregate ancestry-specific results. We evaluated fine-mapping accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency using realistic simulations derived from UK Biobank genotype data, with real-data validation in the All of Us Research Program. Our study revealed that joint modeling approaches achieve improved power and resolution for causal variants shared across populations. In comparison, post-hoc integration is more robust in recovering causal variants present in only a subset of populations by accommodating differences in variant availability. Moreover, methods are generally underpowered in the presence of systematic discrepancies between GWAS summary statistics and external LD reference panels. Motivated by these complementary performance profiles, we propose the multi-ancestry fine-mapping decision strategy, which avoids a priori method selection by adaptively selecting approaches based on locus-level evidence of ancestry-specific variants. Together, our benchmarking and decision strategy offer practical guidance for robust multi-ancestry fine-mapping and highlight the importance of joint modeling that effectively accounts for ancestry-specific variant availability and LD mismatch.

abstract: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics (ST) facilitates the spatial resolution of gene expression profiling; however, many widely used spot-based sequencing platforms capture transcripts from multiple neighboring cells at each location, producing mixed profiles that require accurate cell-type deconvolution. The wavelet-denoised graph attention framework for spatial transcriptomics deconvolution (WDGTA), a graph attention-based framework for ST cell-type deconvolution, was developed and validated on five datasets from two species and four organs. Through the integration of real with pseudo-ST spots, WDGTA introduces a wavelet-based multiscale denoising and reconstruction module, constructs a weighted topological graph using random projection forests, and applies multi-head graph attention to infer cell-type proportions in spatial spots. WDGTA achieved optimal performance in comparison with seven established deconvolution methods. Ablation and discrete wavelet transform (DWT)-specific analyses confirmed the contributions of wavelet denoising, weighted graph construction, and semi-supervised learning. Furthermore, DWT performance remained stable after feature-order perturbation. In mouse brain, cerebellum and ultraviolet radiation (UVR) skin data, WDGTA recovered biologically consistent spatial cell-type patterns and demonstrated robust cross-platform applicability and improved resolution of low-abundance melanocyte signals. Furthermore, it accurately captured melanocyte-associated spatial changes under conditions of UVR exposure and drug intervention. WDGTA provides a unified framework for ST deconvolution across the evaluated tissue contexts. In UVR-exposed skin, it resolved localized melanocyte-associated patterns that were concordant with marker-gene evidence and detected changes associated with UVR exposure and drug treatment. These findings support its use for characterizing spatial cell-type organization and low-abundance cell populations in heterogeneous tissues.

abstract: Abstract Body fluid identification methods have become increasingly well-established, but deconvoluting multi-component mixtures remains a significant challenge. When dealing with complex mixtures, methods based on mRNA coding-region SNPs (cSNPs) still face limitations such as limited polymorphisms of markers and insufficient population specificity. mRNA coding-region microhaplotypes (cMHs), combining tissue specificity with high discrimination power, offer a promising alternative for donor attribution in body fluid stains. In this study, we developed a targeted RNA sequencing panel for East Asian populations, comprising 36 body fluid-specific genes containing 48 cMHs (including 108 cSNPs), along with five genes lacking cMHs. This panel enables both tissue source identification and donor attribution for five types of body fluids and their mixtures. Through specificity evaluation of single-source body fluid stains, we identified six novel body fluid-specific genes. Furthermore, by integrating machine learning algorithms with an in silico mixing strategy, we developed a body fluid classifier that achieved accurate inference for both single-source fluids and complex mixtures. The panel's cumulative discrimination power across the five body fluid types ranged from 0.99568126 (peripheral blood) to 0.99999999 (vaginal secretion). In conclusion, the dual-purpose panel demonstrates robust performance in both tissue source identification and donor attribution for single-source body fluids and complex mixtures.

abstract: Abstract Data sparsity is a central challenge in pervasive computing and human–machine interactive systems, where observations arise unevenly across users, devices, algorithms, and environments. Across recommender interfaces, healthcare monitoring, smart-city mobility, and language-enabled interaction, sparsity can reflect incomplete sensing, constrained exposure, intermittent participation, privacy limits, and heterogeneous event generation. These mechanisms can produce missing or weakly supported instances as well as observable structures such as excess zeros and long-tail frequency distributions; conflating mechanisms with their manifestations can lead to mismatched modelling and evaluation. This survey synthesises 134 studies and develops a source-to-structure diagnostic framework. It distinguishes two mechanism-oriented perspectives—data collection oriented sparsity and user–system interaction oriented sparsity—from a distributional structure oriented perspective that records observable zero-inflated and long-tail patterns without assuming their causes. Six operational forms are connected through a support-based chain from mechanism to observational support, observable structure, and intervention. The roadmap further distinguishes evidence acquisition, bias correction, robust learning under fixed sparsity, and decentralised utilisation, and specifies cross-domain transfer conditions, mechanism- and structure-aware evaluation, and human-centred trade-offs for conditional method selection.

abstract: Abstract Georeferenced time series are central to domains such as urban planning and climate studies, yet insights remain difficult to obtain when patterns span multiple variables and scales. Analysts often seek events —abrupt changes that may co‐occur across variables, space, and time. The Graph Wavelet Transform (GWT) is effective for detecting such changes; however, previous visualization tools have primarily applied it to univariate signals. We introduce ManyWaves , a visual analytics system that applies GWT separately to each variable and integrates the resulting event information in a coordinated multivariate environment. Each variable is modelled as a signal on a shared spatiotemporal graph, and its high‐frequency wavelet coefficients characterize local spatial and temporal changes. A 1D convolutional autoencoder then learns a low‐dimensional representation from these coefficients, which drives linked views: a projection of locations by event similarity, a heatmap summarizing when variables change, and spatial and time‐series views for detailed inspection. Through three case studies—U.S. flight disruptions, traffic and crime in São Paulo, and land‐use change in the Brazilian Legal Amazon—we show how ManyWaves supports the exploration of multivariate events. Expert feedback suggests that the system's event‐oriented views and interactions support sense‐making, while also highlighting the need for onboarding to interpret wavelet‐based representations.

abstract: Abstract The proliferation of highly realistic forged images, driven by advances in generative models such as GANs and diffusion models, poses serious challenges to information security and digital forensics. While existing detection methods leveraging spatial-domain features have shown progress, they often struggle to generalize to ever-evolving forgery techniques–particularly AI-generated content. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Multi-scale Fourier Enhancement Network that integrates frequency-domain analysis with multi-scale feature learning. Our approach incorporates a lightweight Fourier Enhancement Module into a ConvNeXt backbone, enabling the capture of frequency anomalies introduced by forgery operations. Combined with a multi-scale fusion mechanism and a hybrid loss function, the model achieves robust feature learning from local textures to global semantics. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves superior accuracy and robustness while maintaining computational efficiency, and shows promising cross-generator generalization performance on unseen generative sources.

abstract: The problem of covering a two-dimensional region with identical circles of minimal radius (CRICMR) is a classic optimization problem with many relevant real-world applications. However, due to the nonconvexity and the multiply-connected nature of the region to be covered, designing an efficient formulation and solution approach for the problem is very challenging. In this study, we first propose a unified optimization model for two classic variants of the problem (i.e., the CRICMR problems with and without center placement constraints), and then present an effective heuristic algorithm for solving both variants. The proposed model is based on the clipped Voronoi diagram and converts the intractable region coverage problem into the much easier vertex covering problem with respect to the clipped Voronoi polygons. The proposed algorithm incorporates several key components: a two-phase monotonic basin-hopping method; a subregion-based local optimization method; two perturbation operators, and a radius adjustment method for the covering circles. Computational experiments on popular benchmark instances demonstrate the efficiency of our approach, which significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by improving the current best-known solutions for nearly all benchmark instances. abstract: In this work, we propose a preconditioned augmented Lagrangian method (ALM) for solving semidefinite programming (SDP) problems. The preconditioner is implemented via a weighted penalty function in the ALM subproblem, with the weight matrix derived from the projection operator onto the tangent space of the feasible region. This simple yet effective modification significantly accelerates ALM, particularly for ill-conditioned SDPs. By combining the preconditioned ALM with our previously developed feasible method, SDPF, we develop SDPF+, an SDP solver capable of handling convex problems with possibly nonlinear objective functions. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of SDPF+, showing that it can generally outperform other solvers on large-scale SDPs whose optimal solutions exhibit low-rank structure.
