abstract: We study the optimal pricing problem for operations at a seaport terminal within a multimodal transport network, where the terminal operator sets differentiated prices for processing cargoes arriving via and transferred to various modes of transport. The problem incorporates two critical features: (i) the influence of port congestion on cargo suppliers’ terminal selection and (ii) the hierarchical choice structure that predicts how cargo suppliers select transport modes and routes for their cargoes. To capture these features, we formulate the problem as a nonconvex, nonlinear program involving a nested logit choice model and an equilibrium constraint reflecting the congestion effect, which is challenging to solve or analyze. To address this difficulty, we apply a change of variables to reformulate the price-based model as a flow-based model, where cargo flows, rather than prices, are the decision variables, thereby making the model more amenable to analysis. By exploiting the structure of the flow-based model, we derive an optimality equation whose dimension scales only with the number of origin-destination (O/D) pairs, which effectively reduces the computational complexity by avoiding directly handling the numerous variables associated with transport routes. This approach not only applies to seaport revenue management problems that often involve multiple transport modes and a substantial number of routes, but also contributes a structure-exploiting method for addressing a broader class of nonlinear programs involving equilibrium constraints and customer choice models. We show that, for each O/D pair, the optimal mode-dependent prices decompose into a component common across modes plus a mode-specific adjustment. We also establish analytical bounds on the revenue loss induced by misspecifying cargo suppliers’ choice structure. We evaluate the performance of the algorithm by comparing it with several widely used benchmark methods through numerical analysis. Our findings indicate that our algorithm outperforms the benchmark methods in both revenue maximization and runtime. Moreover, we find that accurately modeling the choice structure has a larger impact on revenue than explicitly modeling congestion. abstract: Machine learning and data science techniques have been widely used in practice and have received significant attention. In research settings, business scholars have begun to adopt machine learning as methodological tools. This paper reviews the literature that leverages machine learning-generated measurements to support empirical analysis and yield business insights, where machine learning can reduce reliance on human coding or enable new theoretical perspectives. We summarize the workflow, constructs, and measure structures in these machine learning measure-supported empirical studies. We believe machine learning holds substantial potential to advance business research. History: Accepted by Ram Ramesh, Area Editor for Data Science & Machine Learning. abstract: Extensive simulation studies of reinforcement learning algorithms in pricing environments suggest that it may be possible for them to learn to collude when including a memory of one period. Theoretical analyses of this phenomenon have focused on the setting with two prices, while the simulations have been carried out with up to fifteen prices. Here, we address this gap by analyzing the probability of observing collusion by Decentralized Q-learning in a pricing duopoly with three possible prices and a memory of one period. Using the logit demand model for the payoffs leads to a payoff structure that is a three-action generalization of the iterated PD. Our central question is whether the addition of an intermediate action (or price) between “defection” and “cooperation” increases the likelihood of observing cooperation/collusion. The Decentralized Q-learning algorithm is provably convergent in this environment, and the basins of attraction of its equilibria can be calculated explicitly using Individual Best-Response Graphs. We find that even though the additional action increases the number of collusive equilibria, the likelihood of collusion does not increase. In addition, we find common structure in the possible strategy equilibria, identify conditions for their existence, and refine the notion of collusive strategy equilibria. Finally, we show that introducing fluctuations to the learning process drastically increases the likelihood of collusion, but not to the levels observed when introducing fluctuations in the environment with two prices. Designing effective antitrust policy and detection tools against the threat of algorithmic collusion requires understanding the mechanisms by which algorithms learn to collude. To this end, our results provide new insight into the drivers of collusion among reinforcement learners.

abstract: Abstract Objective Interpretive clinical artificial intelligence (AI), in which a clinician interprets an image or signal and an AI system offers a competing or confirming read, is increasingly routine in radiology, pathology, dermatology, and endoscopy. Oversight of these systems assumes that independent human judgment occurred before AI influence entered the decision. The informatics infrastructure, meaning the electronic health record, its audit logs, and the reporting systems built on them, does not verify this. Discussion We name the missing assurance layer decision integrity, situate it between cybersecurity verification and clinical quality review, and argue it is a measurement construct distinct from diagnostic accuracy. Drawing on the logic of preregistration, we propose a candidate architecture, a minimal six-event record under sequential disclosure, preserving tamper-evident evidence of pre-AI judgment, post-AI revision, and rationale. Conclusion The architecture is a candidate for evaluation, not a validated standard; its purpose is to make clinician independence auditable rather than assumed.

abstract: Abstract Objective Ovarian cancer (OvCa) patients and caregivers face complex, evolving information needs, yet digital health platforms often lack tailoring. This study developed and validated computational personas to support a tailored recommender system (Health E-Librarian with Personalized Recommendations [HELPeR]) and address the cold-start problem, in which limited information about new users reduces the system’s ability to generate relevant recommendations. Materials and Methods We used a mixed-methods design integrating 4 data sources: (1) online OvCa forum posts (n = 457; 60 users), (2) semi-structured interviews with patients and caregivers (n = 20), (3) clinical case notes from a caregiver support program, and (4) expert input from gynecologic oncology nurses. Forum data were manually annotated and analyzed using k-modes clustering to identify user subgroups. Qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis, and findings were integrated to construct and refine personas. Results Five distinct user clusters were identified from forum data. Integration of multi-source data yielded 15 personas (9 patients, 6 caregivers) representing trajectories from diagnosis to end-of-life care. Patient personas captured needs related to symptom management, treatment decision-making, financial concerns, and psychosocial support, while caregiver personas emphasized communication, emotional burden, self-care, and care coordination. Personas reflected dynamic, context-dependent needs and were validated for clinical realism through expert review. Discussion Persona-based modeling provides an interpretable framework for tailored recommendation and approximates digital twin approaches, helping mitigate cold-start limitations. Conclusion Multi-source persona development is a feasible strategy for enabling tailored digital health interventions and improving tailored information delivery in oncology care.

abstract: Abstract Objectives To investigate the longitudinal effects of an ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribe use in primary care on outcomes related to documentation time, note writing patterns, and clinician financial productivity. Materials and Methods We conducted a quasi-experimental study with an interrupted time-series design to ascertain the effect of AI scribe use on note writing time, time outside of scheduled hours (TOSH), pajama time (5:30PM-7:00aM), note length, note closure <24 h, and work relative value units (wRVU). For each primary care clinician (physician, advanced practice provider), date of initial access was day 0; each measure was calculated for 150 days prior (pre-period) and after (post-period) day zero. Results Two hundred and twenty clinicians (mean age = 43.7, 70.9% females; 56.4% physicians) from 36 clinics, conducting 314 845 patient encounters were included. Compared to the pre-period, there was 7% decrease in note writing time at day 0 (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.93, 95% credible interval [CI] [0.89, 0.98]), increasing to 16% decrease by day 150 (IRR 0.84, 95% CI [0.82, 0.87]). There was no change in pajama time, TOSH, or wRVU at day 0; however, at day 150, there was a 19% decrease in pajama time (0.81, 95% CI [0.73, 0.90]), 13% decrease in TOSH (0.87, 95% CI [0.77, 0.98]), and a 2% increase in wRVU (1.02, 95% CI [1.01, 1.04]). At day 0, there was a 5% increase in note closures (1.05, 95% CI [1.02, 1.08]), with no difference to pre-period levels by day 150. There were no changes in note length at day 0 or day 150. Discussion and Conclusion There were persistent changes in AI scribe use measures over time as clinicians situated these tools within their workflows.

abstract: Abstract Objectives Smart healthcare innovations driven by Virtual Human Twin (VHT) technology enable continuous patient monitoring. However, standards to assess their stage of development or a unified framework for performance comparisons are still lacking. This study aims to quantitatively analyze VHT-related studies, evaluate their development levels, and align them to the VHT roadmap. Materials and methods A systematic review guided by the PRISMA methodology was conducted, in which 26 studies representing different stages of VHT development were systematically analyzed. Articles were evaluated against an established 5-level roadmap and classified according to their closest alignment with black box, grey box, or surrogate VHTs. Results A rubric system was developed to assess VHT models to date, and their maturity was analyzed relative to the established roadmap. Among the 26 studies, all 5 roadmap levels were represented. Level 2 (Deductive stage) was the most frequently represented. Levels 4 and 5 (Evolutionary and Explainable stages) were represented only in 3 studies each. Discussion Among the included studies, VHT development appears fragmented, with significant hurdles in building VHTs with advanced functionality. Conclusion The proposed rubric system may serve as an assessment tool to evaluate progress, encourage discussion, and improve experimental approaches for future VHTs, helping address challenges in advancing VHT development along the established roadmap.

abstract: Abstract Objective To systematically review and characterize methodological heterogeneity in sepsis case detection using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III (MIMIC-III) and eICU-CRD databases. Materials and Methods We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed and Web of Science (publication years 2016-2024). Studies were eligible if they applied the SOFA-based Sepsis-3 definition to MIMIC-III or eICU-CRD, provided at least one explicit label-calculation detail, reported a traceable detection rate, and met further criteria detailed in the PRISMA flow diagram. We classified each study by study type and unit of analysis (patients, admissions, or ICU stays) and extracted methodological details on sepsis case detection across 6 domains. For studies with available source code, we additionally examined code structure and repository dependencies to identify methodological decisions across these domains. Results Of 396 publications screened, 64 met inclusion criteria and 12 provided source code. Sepsis detection rates ranged from 3.4% to 65.2% in MIMIC-III and from 9.8% to 47.9% in eICU-CRD. Substantial variability persisted among studies using identical cohort definitions within both databases (MIMIC-III: 16.9%-42.2%; eICU-CRD: 13.9%-31.4%). In a generalized linear mixed model, between-study heterogeneity was extreme (overall τ²≈0.79; 95% prediction interval for a new study’s detection rate 5%–63%), and study-level characteristics—including database, study type, infection detection method, code availability, and unit of analysis—explained only a small proportion of this variance (≈9%), with no characteristic reaching statistical significance. The overall proportion of studies reporting methodological details varied by domain: SOFA calculation (53.1%), infection detection methods (42.2%), temporal windows (37.5%), aggregation methods (26.6%), and missing-data handling (17.2%). Source code analysis identified 321 implementation decisions, revealing heterogeneity in baseline SOFA definitions (SOFA = 0 vs dynamic baseline), temporal windows (infection-centered vs ICU-admission-centered) and infection detection methods (antibiotic-culture matching vs APACHE-based diagnosis). Dependencies among several MIMIC-III repositories suggested propagation of implementation decisions across studies. Discussion Clinically validated sepsis definitions yield substantially different detection rates across studies using identical datasets. Statistical modeling showed that this variability is driven almost entirely by between-study implementation differences rather than sampling error or study characteristics. Conclusion To improve reproducibility in sepsis research and the robustness of sepsis prediction models, we recommend standardized reporting of sepsis case detection methodology and the publication of version-controlled source code.

abstract: Abstract Objectives To evaluate whether increasing agentic architectural complexity via self-reflection or multiagent design improves clinical code status extraction (Do Not Resuscitate [DNR], Do Not Intubate [DNI], Comfort Measures Only [CMO]) across open-source large language models (LLMs) of varying capabilities. Materials and Methods We conducted a controlled cross-model comparison evaluating 3 architectures: (1) single extractor agent, (2) single agent with self-reflection, and (3) sequential multiagent extractor-reviewer system. Four open-source LLMs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, Qwen3.5-27B) were evaluated on 1000 Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV-Note discharge summaries. Ground truth labels were established through a physician-AI dual review with adjudication (Cohen’s κ = 0.98-0.99). Models were evaluated on accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Cohen’s κ, token consumption, and processing latency. McNemar’s test was used for paired comparisons. Results For capable larger models (GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, Qwen3.5-27B), single-agent architectures achieved comparable or superior performance for explicit code status (DNR, DNI) relative to complex systems, whereas multiagent review doubled token consumption and latency without accuracy gains. Reflective self-review significantly impaired MedGemma-27B-IT on DNI extraction (P = .047). For the smaller DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, multiagent review provided statistically significant corrective benefits for DNR (P = .017) and CMO (P < .001), demonstrating a capability-threshold effect, though performance remained below clinically acceptable levels. Discussion Architectural complexity does not enhance extraction performance for capable LLMs, and reflective self-review may cause conservative overcorrection. Multiagent verification value is inversely related to model capability. Conclusion Single-agent LLMs provide optimal accuracy and efficiency for explicit clinical extraction in capable models. Agentic complexity must be matched to both task characteristics and model capability rather than adopted by default.

abstract: The automatic analysis of bird vocalizations holds significant promise for conservation monitoring, ecology, and vocal behavioural studies. Existing bird call classification methods face difficulties in detecting multiple overlapping bird vocalizations. To address this challenge, we propose GraftGIL-Net, a grafting framework based on graph inductive learning networks for bird call classification. Initially, a graph named Mel-Graph is created from the Mel-spectrogram of the audio file using a trained DeepConvNet model. This graph is then fed to the proposed GraftGIL-Net for classification. The proposed method is evaluated on the Xeno-canto bird sound database and achieves a macro F1-score of 0.95.

abstract: The current study involved the ability of deep-learning based noise reduction to generalize to accented-English speech. The deep neural network (DNN) was trained using a large number of different speakers (and different noises) of primarily standard native American English. This model was used to remove background noise from speech produced by 88 speakers having 9 different native-language backgrounds, who spoke English as a second language. The resulting speech was characterized by accents strong enough to substantially affect intelligibility. Objective measures of intelligibility, which reflect acoustic accuracy of the signal following noise reduction, indicated that the DNN generalized to accented speech well. Human-subjects intelligibility testing supported this conclusion. These results are promising in terms of the ability to deploy DNN-based noise reduction in hearing devices to broad populations, including those who receive speech from non-native speakers. Additional objective measures of speech quality indicated that the DNN led to slightly higher subjective sound quality for speech that had lesser accents and was more similar to the speech used for model training. This result suggests that expanding the training set to include accented speech has the potential to improve subjective sound quality of the processed signal.

abstract: The generalized sidelobe canceler (GSC) is a widely used beamforming framework in acoustic signal processing, where constrained optimization is reformulated through a two-path structure consisting of a fixed upper-path beamformer and an adaptive lower path. From a beampattern perspective, this paper revisits the conventional GSC and reveals key limitations caused by mismatches between the upper- and lower-path beampatterns, which can lead to noise amplification and reduced interference suppression, particularly in broadband scenarios. To address these issues, we propose modified GSC-based beamforming designs in which the conventional blocking matrix is replaced by a null beamformer. By increasing beampattern similarity in both magnitude and phase, the proposed structure enables more effective signal subtraction. Based on this formulation, we develop two variants: a fixed beamforming approach that eliminates the adaptive filter in the lower path and an adaptive approach that uses a single adaptive filter with a modified update rule. Simulation results demonstrate improved convergence, robustness, and interference suppression compared to the conventional GSC. The matlab implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/PhanLeSon03/FBSS_ABSS.git.

abstract: Sonic booms generated by supersonic aircraft produce atmospheric pressure waves that can be coupled into the ground and be recorded by seismic networks, providing an alternative means to study their propagation, in particular the landing locations of primary and secondary sonic boom signals. In this study, we evaluate the feasibility of dense seismic networks in Southern California to detect and spatially map sonic booms from aircraft traveling at speeds of Mach 1–1.5, proposed speeds for future commercial supersonic aircraft. Seismic data from supersonic flights over Edwards Air Force Base in 2022 and 2005 were analyzed to identify primary boom signatures, including N- and U-type waves, and secondary boom signatures, including type I and type II waves. Results show that primary and secondary booms, when atmospheric conditions are favorable, are clearly recorded on seismic stations spanning spatial extents of approximately 5000 and 30 000 km2, respectively. This finding demonstrates dense seismic arrays have the potential to record boom signals with sufficient fidelity to ascertain the landing regions and propagation characteristics of both primary and secondary sonic booms, showcasing the feasibility of seismic observations for characterizing acoustic wave propagation from routine supersonic flights.

abstract: This study contributes to a broader research programme examining the characteristics and selection criteria of acoustic pots in the medieval and Renaissance periods. The rationale behind the selection of the resonance frequency of these pots has traditionally been explained by the practice of tapping the pot's neck during manufacture. However, the frequency changes between the potter's shop and insertion into walls, vaults, or domes due to radiation conditions. It is well known in the literature on resonating pipes (e.g., organs) that, due to the inertia of the air in the open termination, the resonance frequency changes according to the insertion. Previous studies have examined baffled pipes, pipes without baffles, and pipes ending in a crown. Here, we use numerical simulation to study the resonance frequency of a Helmholtz resonator neck ended by a hemisphere. This configuration corresponds to an existing case on an archaeological site, while also providing a convenient mathematical model of a neck ending in a baffle with a certain radius of curvature. The article studies the effect of the dome on the frequency for both a Helmholtz resonator and a long pipe. Our results demonstrate that the frequency depends both on the diameter and length of the neck.

abstract: Two essential points of consideration for spherical directivity measurements are the measurement radius and the sound source's location relative to the evaluation surface. When spatial constraints, such as anechoic chamber size, limit the measurement radius, both points may lead to measured near-field directivity patterns deviating from the desired far-field radiation characteristics. To clarify the impact of source placement on near-field and far-field radiation patterns, this work develops far-field magnitude and phase relations between untranslated and translated sources. The resulting theory shows that far-field propagation via acoustical holography is sufficient to correct for source-positioning uncertainties, provided that the measurements incorporate sufficient sampling positions to avoid spatial aliasing. The magnitude equivalence of translated and untranslated far-field directivity patterns also enables an acoustic centering procedure that overcomes previous low-frequency limitations.

abstract: This paper presents a Bayesian geoacoustic inversion method for estimating seabed properties using ship noise in deep water. Two bottom-reflected paths are observed in the processing of low-frequency data recorded by a bottom-moored vertical line array. To accurately represent the observed reflection paths and characterize the thick sediment layer influenced by gravitational compaction, the seabed is parameterized using a continuous-gradient model. Bayesian inversion based on the interference striations is applied to data from the periods before and after the closest point of approach. The Bayesian information criterion is employed to determine the optimal number of sediment layers. Inversion results indicate a total sediment thickness of approximately 460 m, comprising an upper layer with a gradual sound speed gradient (0.46 s−1) and a lower layer with a steep gradient (1.90 s−1). Parameter estimates show consistent agreement with seismic profiles, with the two sediment layers corresponding to the Pleistocene and the Pliocene, respectively. These results demonstrate that the proposed method provides reliable geoacoustic inversion in deep water. Furthermore, they indicate that the sediment structure is better represented by continuous gradients than by discrete homogeneous layers.

abstract: The curved nonlinear internal waves (NIWs) commonly found in shallow-water ocean regions can have significant effects on acoustic propagation. Energy trapped in ducts between waves can be carried over distances of tens of kilometers or more. A three-dimensional feature model for curved NIWs with finite-width waves can produce horizontally tunneling “companion” modes with similar phase patterns to trapped modes, which carry greater energy into the far field than classical tunneling modes. Azimuthal (along-wavefront) wavenumbers and their corresponding mode shapes are presented, and wavenumber approximations obtained from a mode number conservation law compare favorably with benchmark values from the modal dispersion relation. Wavenumbers dependence on NIW radius of curvature is shown, and wavenumber approximations are accurate enough for use in sensitive computations such as modal transmission loss. Transmission loss computations for varying radius of curvature are performed, and the statistical distribution of solutions is examined. Favorable comparisons between this idealized model and a sech2 wave profile suggest that the enhanced tunneling effects of companion modes are realistic. Results for the computations and tests in this paper indicate that the approximation and analysis methods presented are appropriate for a variety of curved waveguide feature models, including those with multiple interfaces.

abstract: In distributed localization of underwater targets, joint time-difference-of-arrival and direction-of-arrival measurements provide an effective means for target localization. However, increased measurement errors under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions can make the approximation errors introduced by the linear treatment of nonlinear observation equations more pronounced, thereby degrading localization performance. To address these issues, an improved localization method based on joint time-difference-of-arrival and direction-of-arrival estimation is proposed. The method introduces auxiliary variables to transform the nonlinear observation equations into a pseudo-linear form, enabling the construction of a weighted least squares problem for estimating the target location. The initial solution is further refined by imposing a projection constraint derived from the geometric relationship between the target and the reference node, thereby reducing the estimation inconsistency arising from the pseudo-linear formulation. On this basis, iterative optimization is employed to obtain a more accurate estimate, thereby extending the effective SNR range. The method achieves high accuracy under high-SNR conditions while maintaining robustness in low-SNR environments. Theoretical analysis shows that the projection-corrected closed-form estimate can achieve the Cramer–Rao lower bound under small noise conditions. Simulation results and processing of SWellEx-96 experimental data verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

abstract: Abstract The Molecular Distance Geometry Problem is essential to structural biology, as it seeks to determine three-dimensional protein structures from partial interatomic distances. Its discretizable subclass (DMDGP) admits an exact combinatorial formulation that enables efficient exploration of the search space. However, in practical settings such as Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, distances are available only within uncertainty bounds, leading to the interval variant ( i DMDGP). We propose a hybrid combinatorial–continuous framework for solving the i DMDGP. The method combines an enumeration process derived from the DMDGP with a continuous refinement stage that minimizes a nonconvex stress function penalizing deviations from admissible distance intervals. This integration supports a systematic exploration guided by discrete structure and local optimization. The formulation incorporates torsion angle intervals and chirality constraints through an atom ordering that preserves protein-backbone geometry. Numerical experiments show that the approach efficiently reconstructs geometrically valid conformations even under wide distance bounds, whereas most existing studies assume narrow ones.

abstract: Purpose: Brain–computer interface (BCI) may support communication and computer interaction through neural signals such as the P300 event-related potential (ERP). As a step toward integrating photographic visual scene displays (VSDs) in BCI, this study examined the feasibility of incorporating contextual, naturalistic scenes in which communication items were embedded asymmetrically. Method: To evaluate the effects of contextual scene use, 24 neurotypical children aged 8–13 years completed three experimental conditions: (1) a contextual scene with asymmetrical item placement, (2) an asymmetrical arrangement of the same items without contextual information, and (3) a standard grid. Electroencephalogram data were analyzed for the N170, P300, and N400 ERP components, and offline (predicted) BCI augmentative and alternative communication accuracy was calculated. Results: The results showed that asymmetry increased frontal and centro-parietal P300 amplitudes, and the scene enhanced occipital N170. Offline BCI performance was similar across the scene and grid conditions, and participants rated the scene as more visually appealing. Conclusion: These findings indicate that asymmetry and contextual embedding within scenes may enhance neural engagement and user experience, providing a preliminary foundation for considering photographic VSDs into pediatric BCI research.

abstract: Purpose: This preliminary investigation occurred across two studies and examined validity, discriminant accuracy, and feasibility of the Sentence Completion Expressive Language Task–Preschool (SCELT-P) for characterizing language production in a neuroimaging environment for typically developing (TD) preschoolers and those with developmental language disorder (DLD). Method: Two separate studies were completed. Study 1 (validity) included 82 preschoolers (50% female; 69 TD, 13 DLD) aged 4;0 (years;months) to 5;11 ( M age = 4;7). All children were assessed using standardized language measures (e.g., Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals Preschool–Second Edition), a play-based language sample (analyzed using Developmental Sentence Scoring), and the 30-item SCELT-P (outside the neuroimaging environment), later streamlined to 20 items (SCELT-P Revised [SCELT-PR]). Study 2 (feasibility) included 14 preschoolers ( M age = 4;9, 43% female; nine TD, five with DLD) that were assessed using the SCELT-P (inside the neuroimaging environment) and functional magnetic resonance imaging using a sparse acquisition approach with a “listen” (passive) and “listen + speak” (active) condition implemented using DirectRT software. Results: In Study 1, the SCELT-P and SCELT-PR demonstrated high reliability, including interrater (intraclass correlation coefficient = .99), test–retest ( r = .86 and .80, respectively), and internal consistency (Cronbach's α > .86 and .83, respectively), and similar strong criterion validity ( r = . 53–.84). Area under the curve analyses (.91) revealed both versions also evidenced fair sensitivity (.88 and .87) and specificity (.85) rates with a cutoff score of 15.5 and 9.5, respectively. In Study 2, 89% of TD preschoolers and 60% of preschoolers with DLD successfully completed the SCELT-P/R inside the neuroimaging environment, with activation maps illustrating relatively similar neurobiological characteristics across preschoolers in some brain regions. Conclusion: The SCELT-P, including its streamlined version, the SCELT-PR, holds promise as a reliable and valid task for including 4- to 5-year-olds in the neuroimaging environment to inform neural and cognitive systems involved in language development. abstract: Purpose: Advances in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and natural language processing have the potential to meaningfully impact language assessment. Despite the increasing availability of these technologies, little is known about their performance in routine assessment tasks such as language sample analysis (LSA), which is commonly used in the identification of developmental language disorder (DLD). This study examined the performance of ASR in transcribing child language samples, as well as the concurrent validity and diagnostic accuracy of metrics derived from an automated LSA system. Method: We used an existing corpus of narrative samples from 66 children with DLD and 285 with typical language (TL), which included audio recordings and transcripts. We conducted automated LSA using the proprietary software LSA+, which integrates ASR and natural language processing. We evaluated transcription accuracy by comparing ASR transcripts to those included in the corpus. We then examined associations between language ability metrics from ASR and manual transcripts, as well as the diagnostic accuracy of each, by using LSA+ as a common means of analysis for all transcripts. Results: ASR produced less accurate transcripts for children with DLD than for those with TL and for younger children. Despite differences in transcription accuracy, automated LSA measures exhibited positive correlations with their manual counterparts, ranging from r = .79 to .98. Manual LSA measures in isolation exhibited better diagnostic accuracy than that of their automated counterparts. However, composite models with multiple automated metrics yielded the highest accuracy when including mean length of utterance, number of different words, and total number of words, in addition to ASR-derived mean length of speech segment and pauses per word. Discussion: Full automation of LSA demonstrates the potential to improve the efficiency and robustness of language assessment, particularly when utilizing composite measures. Despite its advantages, automated LSA may result in inaccurate estimates of language ability if used without consideration of its limitations. Continued examination of ASR and related technologies is needed to better understand their efficacy across languages, ages, and types of communication disorders.

abstract: Purpose: The three-alternative forced-choice design of the spectral-temporally modulated ripple test (SMRT) may capture both auditory and neurocognitive functioning. The relationships between neurocognitive functions and SMRT performance remain unexplored in middle-aged and older adults, as does the degree to which hearing loss may affect these relationships. This study hypothesized that better neurocognitive functions and better hearing would predict better SMRT performance and that hearing loss and neurocognitive functions would interact in contributing to SMRT performance. Method: Data were collected from 81 adults recruited from a single tertiary care medical center with hearing abilities ranging from normal hearing to profound hearing loss. Relationships were examined among SMRT performance; unaided pure-tone average (PTA) at 500, 1000, and 2000 Hz; age; nonverbal reasoning (Raven's Progressive Matrices [Raven's]); and short-term memory capacity (visual forward digit span). Results: Bivariate analyses revealed that PTA, digit span, and Raven's scores were significantly associated with SMRT performance, whereas age was not. Multivariable linear regression confirmed these three as independent, significant predictors; age again was not. Interaction terms of PTA × Digit Span and PTA × Raven's were not significant predictors of SMRT performance. Conclusions: Neurocognitive functions of nonverbal reasoning and short-term memory capacity, as well as hearing ability, independently contribute to SMRT performance. Nonsignificant interactions suggest that the neurocognitive effects on SMRT are constant across degrees of hearing loss. These findings support ongoing use of SMRT in middle-aged and older adults with hearing loss, although the independent effects of neurocognitive functions should be accounted for, or at least considered, when interpreting SMRT performance. abstract: Purpose: Narratives show vulnerability in children with developmental language disorder (DLD) cross-linguistically. However, certain narrative measures revealing significant deficits in English and European DLD literature have been studied primarily in preschoolers, with limited evidence in school-aged children and no data in Cantonese. We examine features of vulnerability in narrative production of school-aged children learning a major Chinese language, Cantonese. Method: Twenty-five children with DLD ( M age = 9;7 [years;months]) and age-matched typically developing (TD) peers ( M age = 9;8) were assessed using the Cantonese Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives (MAIN) in story retelling and storytelling. Their narrative competence across macrostructure, microstructure, and internal state term measures were analyzed at group and individual diagnostic accuracy levels. Results: Both expressive macrostructure and microstructure showed significant TD/DLD group differences, indicating story structure (SS), story complexity (SC), syntactic complexity, and grammaticality are vulnerable in monolingual Cantonese-speaking school-aged children with DLD. No significant TD/DLD group differences were registered in number of different words, mean length of utterance, productivity measures (total number of utterances, total number of words), or internal state terms. For diagnostic accuracies, SS and syntactic complexity reached acceptable sensitivity (91.7% and 83.3%, respectively) but limited specificity (41.7% and 70.8%, respectively); SC and grammaticality showed marginal sensitivity and specificity (both 70.8%). Conclusions: This study confirms SS, SC, grammaticality, and syntactic complexity—but not productivity—as features of vulnerability in narrative production of Cantonese-speaking school-aged children with DLD. The exploratory diagnostic accuracy results support using narrative measures in combination with other assessments for diagnosis. Future studies should examine younger and larger samples to further document these vulnerability features and evaluate the clinical utility of narrative measures at earlier developmental stages.

abstract: ABSTRACT Solutions and business architects play a fundamental role in the process of selecting software solutions that satisfy their organizations' objectives and needs to implement a change. These practitioners are often faced with the challenge of selecting the most suitable software among a set of candidate solutions. For that, they often perform a comparative study based on a set of criteria to select the software that best meets the specific needs of their organizations and customers. The software selection is a decision process that plays a crucial role in organizations' digital transformation. However, existing methods have limitations related to their usability and implementation complexity. This paper provides architecture practitioners with a novel method that automatically prioritizes software solutions in order to select the most suitable one. The prioritization process of the solutions is based on: (i) the functional requirements they implement and (ii) the desired goals (business objectives and non‐functional requirements) they satisfy. The proposed method is goal‐oriented. It uses the Goal‐oriented Requirement Language (GRL) that links the candidate software to the requirements to be implemented and the goals to be met. The use of GRL allows the method to automatically compute satisfaction scores that measure the effectiveness of candidate software solutions in implementing requirements and satisfying the desired goals. The satisfaction score is used to rank the software solutions. An experimental study was conducted to evaluate the method's usability. Results demonstrated its effectiveness and alignment with expert expectations in solutions, business architecture, and business analysis.

abstract: ABSTRACT One of the effects of COVID‐19 was that software engineers were forced to work remotely, in many cases without prior experience, which may have led to a number of challenges for projects and organizations, along with developers' well‐being. Several work styles were considered after the pandemic, because not only did teleworking persist but new forms of work emerged, for which neither organizations nor employees were prepared. These new modalities have led to challenges that have not yet been sufficiently addressed in the existing literature, mainly because they are relatively recent phenomena. The aim of this paper is to analyze the risks that remote or hybrid working can pose to software development and examine them from the perspective of the company, the project itself, and employees. Once the problems have been identified, it is important to analyze them from the point of view of a software engineer's personality and assess the likelihood of these challenges arising according to the working model used. It is also essential to find strategies with which to mitigate these challenges. These are the objectives of this paper, which aims to help project managers and developers carry out hybrid or remote software development efficiently and ensure their employees' well‐being. To achieve these objectives, a mixed‐methods approach comprising five stages was adopted: a systematic mapping review to identify and categorize the factors affecting software engineers, a survey of 184 practitioners to validate and refine these factors, a second survey examining the perceived impact of different work modalities on productivity and associated risks, and an evaluation of our framework (main contribution of this paper) through semi‐structured interviews with 10 practitioners.

abstract: Abstract Within the legal domain, named entity recognition (NER) is an essential pre-processing tool for important tasks such as information extraction and redaction. Research to date has focused on rule-based approaches or machine learning strategies that require significant time and effort to train through labelled corpora. Large, multi-purpose generative large language models (LLMs) have been successfully employed on natural language processing (NLP) tasks with no prior supervised training and may represent a way forward in addressing these existing bottlenecks. Despite promising results in certain NLP use cases, the Few-Shot LLM performance on unfamiliar, domain-specific NER tasks has, to date, remained uncertain. In this legal clause NER task, we evaluate a Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategy for OpenAI’s GPT-4 LLM on a new CUAD-NER dataset that we have repurposed for the task of Person and Organisation entity identification. In a comparative study, we demonstrate that the GPT4 + Few-Shot CoT prompt strategy outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving a 5% percentage point improvement in Micro F1 score over the best performing BERT base (cased) competitor. This study also takes the novel approach of assessing the business feasibility of deploying each of these machine learning models through a detailed cost–benefit analysis that measures the trade-off between performance metrics and low and high usage running costs.

abstract: Abstract Digital asset markets are expanding but remain difficult to evaluate, particularly for retail investors who face information overload, unstructured disclosures, and limited regulatory safeguards. Traditional due diligence methods often fail to capture the complexity of blockchain-based projects, exposing investors to misrepresentation and fraud. At the same time, LLMs have shown remarkable results on analyzing large information quantities. Thus, this paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can enhance digital asset assessments by providing inspectable, automated, and low-cost decision support. Using a Design Science Research methodology, we developed a framework and a prototype tool to apply LLM-based evaluation to token-offering whitepapers, evaluated across 1,139 generated runs covering 29 token offerings. We compared different content processing approaches, from raw document analysis to aspect-focused summarization, and tested prompting strategies including Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought reasoning. Our findings show a nuanced pattern. On aggregate quantitative metrics, structured summarization combined with Chain-of-Thought prompting achieves the lowest rating error, although differences in rank correlation between configurations are not statistically resolvable given the number of projects evaluated; aspect-focused summarization structures criterion-specific evidence and candidate red flags explicitly, but its rating error is higher and the interpretability of this representation was not independently evaluated. To address the single-model limitation, we added a lightweight multi-model robustness check using two small open-source models on a matched subset of cases; the results suggest that the observed optimism bias is not specific to the original closed LLM, although performance still varies across model configurations. Overall agreement between model and expert ratings remains limited, which suggests that LLMs are better understood as decision-support tools for screening and explanation than as substitutes for expert judgment. The study therefore contributes a design-oriented due diligence artifact and a dependence-aware evaluation of how summarization and prompting choices affect calibration, output-level inspectability, and validity boundaries in digital asset assessment.

abstract: Abstract We give a new formulation of Turing reducibility in terms of higher modalities, inspired by an embedding of the Turing degrees in the lattice of subtoposes of the effective topos discovered by Hyland. In this definition, higher modalities play a similar role to I/O monads or dialogue trees in allowing a function to receive input from an external oracle. However, in homotopy type theory (HoTT), they have better logical properties than monads: they are compatible with higher types, and each modality corresponds to a reflective subuniverse that under suitable conditions is itself a model of HoTT. We give synthetic proofs of some basic results about Turing reducibility in cubical type theory making use of two axioms of Markov induction and computable choice . Both axioms are variants of axioms already studied in the effective topos. We show they hold in certain reflective subuniverses of cubical assemblies, demonstrate their use in some simple proofs in synthetic computability theory using modalities and show they are downwards absolute for oracle modalities. These results have been formalised using cubical mode of the Agda proof assistant. We explore some first connections between Turing reducibility and homotopy theory. This includes a synthetic proof that two Turing degrees are equal as soon as they induce isomorphic permutation groups on the natural numbers, making essential use of both Markov induction and the formulation of groups in HoTT as pointed, connected, 1-truncated types. We also give some simple non-topological examples of modalities in cubical assemblies based on these ideas, to illustrate what we expect higher-dimensional analogues of the Turing degrees to look like.

abstract: Abstract Despite their success, Deep Learning (DL) models are susceptible to spurious correlations. These are accidental correlations between non-predictive features of the training dataset and the target label, leading to models that do not generalise well to samples without such spurious correlations. We propose to address this failure mode by extending and improving an existing method for spurious correlation robustness — UnLearning from Experience (ULE). ULE trains two models in parallel; a biased model is encouraged to learn the spurious correlations, while a separate debiased model is trained to solve the same task while avoiding learning the same behaviour as the first, thus avoiding learning the spurious correlations. A weakness of ULE is that it treats every training example identically, regardless of whether or not it contains a spurious correlation. Therefore, ULE does not make optimal use of the training data, leading to worse-than-necessary performance. To address this weakness, we introduce Weighted UnLearning from Experience (wULE), which modifies the original ULE loss function to reweight the components depending on whether a training sample likely contains spurious correlations. Hence, we explore two methods for identifying training samples likely to contain spurious correlations. We test our approach using several well-known spurious correlation robustness benchmarks — Waterbirds, CelebA, UrbanCars and MultiNLI. Our novel wULE method outperforms the original ULE in all cases and achieves Worst-Group Accuracy (WGA) results comparable to the best methods in the spurious correlation robustness literature.

abstract: In an ideal world, authors would report clearly and transparently exactly what they conducted. In reality, reporting is often incomplete, and key elements of research conduct are frequently missing from manuscripts. Reporting guidelines were developed to address this problem by helping authors identify what should be reported. These guidelines have been highly valuable for authors, but they are not well suited for appraising reporting during peer review or editorial assessment despite common use. This is because authors and appraisers have different needs: authors require a comprehensive guide for writing, whereas appraisers need a tool that is concise, repeatable, and easy to use. We therefore propose the development of reporting appraisal tools: operationalised tools designed specifically to assess whether a paper has reported the minimum essential elements of a study. To support their development, we present 10 simple rules.

abstract: Analyses routinely conducted in both fundamental research and biomedical studies often report aggregate signals derived from heterogeneous mixtures of cells. These mixtures reflect the intrinsic anatomical and functional complexity of the tissues and organs from which they are derived. Such bulk measurements obscure cell-specific signals, thereby hindering accurate interpretation of the underlying biological processes. Here, we introduce CLIMB and CLIFF, a two-step machine-learning framework that deconvolves bulk RNA-seq into cell-type composition and expression, and then resolves bulk drug sensitivity measurements into cell subtype- and single-cell-specific profiles. We first validate CLIMB using in-vitro mixtures of leukemic cell lines with experimentally known cell-type proportions, then extend this validation to large-scale, cross-dataset pseudo-bulk analyses built from independent scRNA-seq references across two disease contexts and five cancer types — mimicking the reference-to-target mismatches encountered in real applications — and show that CLIMB accurately infers the cellular composition of bulk samples, outperforming state-of-the-art bulk deconvolution methods. We emphasize CLIMB’s effectiveness in acute myeloid leukemia, where it offers highly accurate estimation of leukemic stem cell fractions across three test datasets and three patient cohorts. We then validate CLIFF, our algorithm for estimating cell subtype- and single-cell-specific drug sensitivity, first on the same in-vitro cell line mixtures using experimentally measured drug responses, and then through in-depth, realistic-scale pseudo-bulk simulations. We applied our deconvolution strategy to the beatAML cohort dataset, currently the most extensive database of ex-vivo drug screening data. This analysis generated a cell subtype–resolved drug sensitivity landscape for 121 compounds, revealing multiple compounds putatively active against leukemic stem cells, including midostaurin, A-674563, SNS-032, and foretinib. Collectively, our work introduces a general computational framework for resolving bulk functional measurements at cell-type and single-cell resolution, providing an attractive new computational tool for drug development and precision medicine.

abstract: We provide a general theoretical explanation for a longstanding result in spatial ecology: weak dispersal among habitat patches promotes local species richness. Using analytical approximations of spatial Lotka–Volterra competition models, we show that local species persistence in heterogeneous landscapes can be expressed as the balance between the total density across patches and the local exclusion rate. We further demonstrate that local multispecies coexistence is governed by the feasibility domain, linking spatial coexistence to a structural property of nonspatial competitive systems. Together, these results explain why weak dispersal increases local species richness and why this effect strengthens with the number of available patches, i.e., landscape size. We test these predictions using numerical simulations and find that the theory breaks down only when both dispersal and competitive interactions are very strong, in which case dispersal has a unimodal effect on coexistence. In contrast, landscape size retains a positive effect on coexistence whenever an effect is detectable. We then apply the theory to long-term data from a natural metacommunity of microcrustaceans. We detect strong competition among species and find no detectable effect of dispersal rate on local coexistence, whereas species co-occurrence increases with local landscape size, as predicted by theory. Together, our results identify how dispersal, interaction strength, and landscape size jointly regulate local species richness in competitive systems.

abstract: Abstract Data constraints are important business rules that specify the values allowed or required for the data used in a software system. These constraints are typically described in textual software artifacts ( e.g., requirements, developer documents, user manuals, etc. ). In this paper, we focus on automating the task of identifying data constraints in natural language software documents. In order to automate this task, we first study how data constraints are described in natural language. Specifically, we studied 546 data constraints described in the natural language artifacts of nine software systems. We uncovered and documented nine linguistic discourse patterns that stakeholders use to describe data constraints in natural language. We cast the constraint identification and extraction as a text matching and classification problem. We explore the suitability of traditional machine learning techniques, using the discourse patterns we discovered, together with other linguistic elements, as features, for automatically classifying sentence fragments as data constraint descriptions. The best combination of features and learner achieves 63.63% precision and 61.40% recall (62.34% F1). Automating the extraction of data constraints from natural language text is essential for automating their traceability to code, test generation, compliance analysis, etc.

abstract: Abstract Embodied artificial intelligence—which involves agents perceiving, reasoning, and acting within physical environments—represents a new frontier towards artificial general intelligence. This study explores the evolving landscape of embodied intelligence, and presents a comprehensive survey on leveraging reinforcement learning (RL) to enhance embodied intelligence, systematically addressing the evolution from single-task performance in controlled settings to sophisticated cross-environment and cross-task capabilities. The study delves into several virtuoso capabilities, such as morphological intelligence (MI), human-like values and ethics, spontaneous reward generation, and reflective equilibrium. These capabilities are essential for developing adaptable, ethical, and intelligent embodied agents capable of navigating complex real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the study identifies and analyzes critical barriers in embodied RL, including sample efficiency, generalization and transferability, safety and robustness, real-time learning and adaptation, and interpretability and transparency. For each of these barriers, we offer an overview of current approaches and propose potential avenues for future research.

abstract: ABSTRACT Modern cloud infrastructures must deliver energy‐efficient, high‐performance services while meeting Quality of Service (QoS) guarantees. However, dynamic workloads and heterogeneous hardware often create resource imbalances across hosts, triggering unnecessary virtual machine (VM) migrations, wasting energy, and increasing Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an Energy‐Convergent migration framework for Dynamic VM Consolidation (DVMC) that integrates the Estimated Imbalance Degree (EID) with a probabilistic SLA Violation Detection Scheme (SDS). Our approach prioritizes migration using VM categorization with weight‐based criticality assessment. It employs mathematical models for demand estimation, Markov‐based load redistribution, bottleneck detection, forecasting, and energy‐aware migration planning. Formal theoretical analysis establishes the correctness of the framework, while efficient algorithms enable practical deployment under diverse cloud workloads. The proposed method accurately identifies host‐level imbalances and suppresses transient migrations through a unified threshold‐driven strategy. This approach enhances system stability and resource utilization. Experiments on OpenStack and CloudSim demonstrate average reductions of up to in energy consumption, in SLA violations, and in migrations compared with state‐of‐the‐art baselines, with the differences confirmed statistically at . Statistical and sensitivity analyses further confirm robustness and practical applicability.

abstract: ABSTRACT Context Pull requests play a pivotal role in the software development life‐cycle, and they produce an abundance of metrics about how contributors and reviewers make decisions within the pull‐based development model. Previous authors make analyses at the individual pull request level, which faces many challenging issues with the scarcity and noisiness of input data, and which yields signals that are difficult to compare between repositories. Objective This study investigates whether signals measured at the repository level characterize developer behavior more robustly than per‐pull‐request measures, and whether such signals generalize across hosting platforms and development contexts. We target two behaviors in particular: how review time responds to code complexity, and how concentrated reviewing is between pairs of developers. Methods We compare four sources of pull request data: Atlassian Bitbucket and Atlassian GitHub repositories from Atlassian Corporation Plc, both publicly available, and the Avatar and ISM/VET Bitbucket project repositories from J.P. Morgan. We first use an augmented Gaussian Mixture Model to model review time against code complexity, bucketed by meaningful lines of code. We then use a graph‐theoretical construction of authors and reviewers to analyze reviewer selection behavior between pairs of developers, from which we construct an aggregate index of overly co‐reviewing behavior and track it over a rolling window across a period of two years. Results Our mixture models fit the data well, and we leverage them to explore and explain instances where code complexity increases, but review time does not. Our index helps in identifying periods of high co‐reviewership, and recovers known episodes in the J.P. Morgan repositories in which single‐reviewer approval of large pull requests was expected. Conclusion Repository‐level signals sidestep the data scarcity and noise that constrain analyses at the individual pull request level, and they yield measures that can be compared across repositories. The inclusion of a public, open‐source GitHub dataset alongside closed‐source Bitbucket projects demonstrates that the methodology generalizes across platforms and development contexts.

abstract: ABSTRACT Background The deployment of soft sensors, data‐based models that estimate unobservable or costly variables from available sensor data, remains limited in IoT infrastructures by the resource constraints of IoT devices and the complexity of managing model lifecycles at scale. Objective This work presents a novel architecture that enables the end‐to‐end transformation, distribution and execution of soft sensors on IoT embedded devices. Methods The proposed approach leverages Kafka‐ML, a framework for managing ML models and data streams, which has been extended to orchestrate the end‐to‐end lifecycle of soft sensors in real time via IoT data streams. By enabling local inference on IoT devices, the system reduces reliance on cloud connectivity during operation: while initial deployment, model updates, and lifecycle orchestration via Kafka‐ML require network access, local inference allows the estimation of complex variables even when subsequent connectivity is unreliable or intermittent. The approach has been evaluated in two representative scenarios, non‐intrusive load monitoring (NILM) and water quality monitoring, each with different demands regarding communications overhead and accuracy. Results The automated quantization pipeline yields negligible accuracy degradation for the NILM scenario (MAE shifted from 2.836 to 2.837) and an acceptable performance trade‐off for water quality monitoring (MAE rose from 0.53 to 0.82 mg/L), while reducing inference latency by up to 4.6× compared to remote inference. Conclusions These results demonstrate the framework's capability to automate the deployment of distributed, autonomous, and privacy‐preserving soft sensors across heterogeneous monitoring scenarios.

abstract: Serverless workflows are commonly modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) composed of fine-grained functions. While this design promotes modularity and programming flexibility, it also incurs frequent inter-function communication. To alleviate this performance overhead, function fusion has been explored to co-locate and execute communicating functions within a shared container instance. However, existing approaches fail to account for the time-varying trade-off between communication latency reduction and resource overprovisioning arising from path uncertainty in dynamic serverless workflows, making it difficult to sustain high resource efficiency over time. In this paper, we propose a new adaptive function fusion strategy that dynamically reconstructs serverless workflows by adjusting communication schemes between functions in response to changing workflow invocations. Realizing this strategy, however, requires jointly optimizing function fusion and per-instance configuration, a problem with a combinatorial search space, while managing the substantial overhead of switching fusion schemes at runtime. To address these challenges, we design AdaFuse, a novel system for dynamic serverless workflows. AdaFuse jointly optimizes function fusion and instance reconfiguration through an efficient beam-search–based algorithm to optimize the end-to-end resource allocation. With the optimized fusion scheme, AdaFuse employs a fluid migration mechanism that incrementally transitions the workflow deployment while seamlessly redirecting incoming workloads. Evaluations across diverse benchmarks show that AdaFuse reduces resource allocation by up to 49.4% compared to baselines, without compromising SLO attainment.

abstract: Cloud data centers increasingly rely on device virtualization to share high-bandwidth network adapters and accelerators among virtual machines (VMs). Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV) exposes Virtual Functions (VFs) directly to guest VMs, but the Input/Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) on the host processor becomes a bottleneck as the number of VFs grows: its small translation lookaside buffer (TLB) causes severe throughput degradation. Meanwhile, because the hypervisor cannot determine which guest memory regions are used for Direct Memory Access (DMA), it must pin the entire VM memory, preventing memory overcommitment and wasting physical resources. Existing solutions, including Address Translation Services (ATS), the Page Request Interface (PRI), and software-emulated virtual IOMMUs, suffer from compatibility, deployment, or CPU overhead limitations. We propose DMMU, a Device MMU system implemented on programmable SmartNICs that addresses both the IOMMU translation bottleneck and the memory-pinning barrier to overcommitment, with minimal host software modification and zero guest awareness. DMMU introduces two techniques: combo-DMA , which dynamically routes address translations between the IOMMU and an on-device translation engine depending on IOMMU load, and direct-PRI , which enables the SmartNIC to issue page fault requests directly to a host-side driver, bypassing the multi-layer emulation path of conventional PRI in virtualized environments. We implement DMMU through a microcode update to a commodity dual-port 100G NIC and evaluate it on Intel Skylake and Ice Lake servers. With a representative 120-VF configuration, DMMU improves NIC throughput by 65% and reduces IOTLB misses by 38 × compared to the baseline IOMMU. DMMU also enables reliable memory overcommitment with device passthrough, achieving near-baseline Redis performance at a 1.35 × overcommitment ratio.

abstract: Singular value decomposition (SVD) is a fundamental matrix factorization in scientific computing and data analysis, but computing it efficiently on modern GPUs remains challenging. Full SVD provides strong numerical robustness but is often expensive for large matrices, whereas randomized SVD (RSVD) improves performance but may exhibit accuracy variability, especially when the target rank is unknown or the singular spectrum decays slowly. To address this challenge, we propose UnifaSVD, a unified and adaptive framework for high-performance and numerically reliable SVD on GPUs. UnifaSVD combines a numerically stable Householder QB (HQB) factorization for numerical rank estimation with a unified EVD-based SVD backend for efficient computation of the required singular values and vectors. Its adaptive architecture supports full-rank, low-rank, and unknown-rank matrices by dynamically selecting an appropriate computational path according to matrix characteristics and user-specified numerical requirements. Rather than relying on a fixed decomposition strategy, UnifaSVD integrates efficient factorization, adaptive rank handling, and lightweight refinement within a single framework. Experimental results show that UnifaSVD achieves numerical accuracy close to full SVD while delivering substantially higher performance across a wide range of tested cases. By automating algorithm selection based on matrix properties and numerical requirements, UnifaSVD provides a robust and efficient solution for SVD on modern GPU architectures.

abstract: Deep learning (DL) compilers rely on cost models and auto-tuning to optimize tensor programs for target hardware. However, existing approaches depend on large offline datasets, incurring high collection costs and offering suboptimal transferability across platforms. In this paper, we introduce TCL , a novel efficient and transferable compiler framework for fast tensor program optimization across diverse hardware platforms to address these challenges. Specifically, TCL is built on three core enablers: (1) the RDU Sampler , a data-efficient active learning strategy that selects only 10% of tensor programs by jointly optimizing R epresentativeness, D iversity, and U ncertainty, substantially reducing data collection costs while maintaining near-original model accuracy; (2) a new Mamba-based cost model that efficiently captures long-range schedule dependencies while achieving a favorable trade-off between prediction accuracy and computational cost through reduced parameterization and lightweight sequence modeling; and (3) a continuous knowledge distillation framework that effectively and progressively transfers knowledge across multiple hardware platforms while avoiding the parameter explosion and data dependency issues typically caused by traditional multi-task learning. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of each individual enabler and the holistic TCL framework. When optimizing a range of mainstream DL models on both CPU and GPU platforms, TCL achieves, on average, 16.8 × and 12.48 × faster tuning time, and 1.20 × and 1.13 × lower inference latency, respectively, compared to Tenset-MLP.

abstract: With the stagnation of single-threaded performance, the need for optimizations targeting sequential code performance is greater than ever before. Modern workloads have also been growing in code footprint, exposing a bottleneck in the processor front-end, specifically its inability to maintain a sufficiently high fetch throughput to saturate available execution units. To address them, two optimizations exist in modern processors: (1) Fetch-Directed Instruction Prefetching (FDIP) and (2) the micro-op cache ( μ op cache), both of which improve fetch throughput leading to improved overall performance. However, since they target the same code regions, in the presence of FDIP, the μ op cache becomes mostly redundant as a performance optimization. abstract: Spatial accelerators can significantly enhance the computational performance of deep neural networks (DNNs) by mapping each layer across spatial and temporal dimensions. However, state-of-the-art mapping tools predominantly rely on perfect factorization mapping (PFM), which restricts tile sizes to exact divisors of tensor dimensions and may overlook high-quality mappings in the broader design space. To address this limitation, we propose MARS, the first efficient exploration framework designed for Ruby space. Ruby space is defined as a generalized mapping space that relaxes the factor-only constraint by allowing any integer tile size within the valid range of a dimension. MARS first models the coupling of partitioning, scheduling, and hardware resource constraints in Ruby space as a constrained optimization problem. It then relaxes the discrete mapping space into a continuous domain and employs a combination of linear programming and a genetic algorithm to rapidly obtain high-quality candidate mappings. Experimental results on representative DNN models show that MARS achieves a reduction of \(15\% \) to \(65\% \) in energy-delay product compared to state-of-the-art methods on average. Furthermore, MARS demonstrates superior exploration efficiency and consistently better mapping quality.

abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) for time series forecasting introduces unique challenges due to the mismatch between continuous time series tokens and the discrete word tokens LLMs are trained on. While LLMs have shown success on natural language tasks, aligning time series tokens with the semantic space of LLMs while preserving both accuracy and interpretability remains an open problem. Existing reprogramming and prompt-based approaches often generate word embeddings that are misaligned with or semantically irrelevant to the corresponding time series. For example, a segment with an increasing trend may be mapped to words like ”mirror” or ”keyboard”, which makes them hard to interpret. To bridge the gap, we propose MLTA-LLM, a Multi-Level Text Alignment framework for time series forecasting with LLMs. MLTA-LLM decomposes time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components, each of which is aligned with semantic anchor embeddings or text prototype embeddings. This component-specific alignment forces the LLM to process time series data through structured, interpretable representations. In addition, we integrate conformal prediction to provide statistically rigorous prediction intervals for uncertainty quantification. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that MLTA-LLM not only improves forecasting accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines but also yields more interpretable representations and better-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted great attention in both academic and industrial communities in recent years. Numerous survey studies have covered various aspects of LLMs, such as learning strategies, applications, alignment, explainability, and evaluation. However, little headway has been made in reviewing data-related aspects for LLMs, despite data being recognized as a key factor contributing to the emergence of the LLMs era. A wide range of data optimization algorithms and techniques are employed in LLMs’ training and application processes. These techniques often originate from diverse deep learning domains, with their theoretical inspirations and heuristic motivations appearing unrelated to each other. This study aims to develop a comprehensive framework for LLMs’ data optimization techniques to enhance data utilization and efficiency. We first discuss data challenges in LLMs’ training and inference. Second, we summarize data perception dimensions for evaluating LLMs’ data properties. These dimensions primarily include quality, difficulty, diversity, and redundancy, laying a foundation for subsequent optimization. Third, existing optimization techniques are reviewed and categorized into four groups: data selection, augmentation, reweighting, and others. Fourth, we analyze interconnections between these categories. Finally, we identify key challenges and future directions for LLMs’ data optimization compared with conventional deep learning approaches.

abstract: Transmission delays are inherent in silicon photonic integrated circuits (PICs) and have a significant impact on their dynamic behavior and system-level performance. However, conventional modeling and simulation approaches often overlook or inadequately account for these delays, limiting accuracy and efficiency in circuit-level analysis. This paper presents a delay-aware macromodeling methodology that explicitly extracts time delays from frequency-domain responses and incorporates them into a compact pole-residue representation. In contrast to traditional techniques such as complex vector fitting (CVF), which approximate delay effects indirectly and often require a large number of poles, resulting in increased model complexity, reduced simulation efficiency, and potential causality violations, the proposed method captures delays explicitly and compactly without compromising accuracy or physical consistency. To enable integration into circuit simulation workflows, we introduce an efficient Verilog-A implementation of the proposed model, along with practical strategies for representing time delays within standard electronic-photonic co-simulation environments. The proposed approach is validated using three categories of passive PIC structures: waveguides, feedforward multi-path circuits, and resonant (loop-based) circuits, demonstrating superior compactness, simulation speed, and accuracy compared to conventional modeling techniques. These results highlight the method’s potential for scalable and high-fidelity modeling of PICs in hybrid electronic-photonic circuit and system design.

abstract: High-Level Synthesis (HLS) design productivity is often constrained by manual, expert-driven pragma tuning and the difficulty of balancing performance optimization with strict hardware resource limits. While automated Design Space Exploration (DSE) has been extensively studied, many existing approaches rely on open-loop estimation models or substantial training data, which can lead to physically unrealizable designs under tight resource budgets. In this work, we propose Reflex-HLS , a training-free agentic framework that formulates HLS optimization as a closed-loop, feedback-driven process grounded in physical synthesis outcomes. Reflex-HLS integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) within a Planner–Actor–Critic architecture, where optimization decisions are iteratively refined based on hardware-in-the-loop feedback from the vendor toolchain, ensuring physical realizability throughout the optimization process. Experimental results on PolyBench and MachSuite benchmarks, validated through full Vivado synthesis and implementation, demonstrate that Reflex-HLS achieves speedups of up to 48.41 × (e.g., on jacobi-2d ) while strictly adhering to device resource constraints. Further evaluations across regular, irregular, and structured workloads show that the proposed framework generalizes beyond conventional compute kernels. Comparative studies against representative open-loop DSE methods, large foundation models operating without hardware feedback, and closed-loop heuristic search highlight the trade-offs among optimization paradigms, with Reflex-HLS producing more deployable and resource-efficient designs under tight resource budgets in the evaluated cases.

abstract: As advanced process nodes continue to scale, heterogeneous integration technologies such as 2.5D/3D packaging, chiplets, and high-bandwidth memory have been widely adopted. However, these advances introduce substantially higher power densities, more complex interconnection structures, and increasingly diverse material systems. The resulting localized hotspots raise reliability concerns such as electromigration, thermomechanical stress, and structural warpage, making layout-driven thermal simulation with balanced accuracy and efficiency essential for rapid design iterations. This paper proposes AceTherm, an automated thermal simulation framework driven by Graphic Data System (GDS) layout and Process Design Kit (PDK) process parameters, which integrates non-conformal finite element method with customized sparse-matrix solvers. By exploiting the layered structure of the chip architecture, the simulation domain is sampled and discretized with a non-conformal mesh and high-resolution material mapping, significantly reducing degrees of freedom (DOFs) while preserving accuracy. The mesh division and sampling resolution provide a two-level control for trading off accuracy and speed, and the convergence and error behavior are analyzed to characterize the discrete scheme of AceTherm. Exploiting the structural properties of the resulting coefficient matrix, AceTherm employs supernodal sparse Cholesky factorization to accelerate the solution process. Notably, the symbolic factorization can be reused across multiple thermal load scenarios when the mesh pattern remains unchanged. Numerical experiments show that the proposed method achieves a 104.6 × speedup over the conventional COMSOL solution and reaches up to 539.2 × in repeated or preset-parameter simulations, while maintaining the average temperature error below 1 K. The combination of high computational speed, layer-aware modeling, and sub-Kelvin accuracy positions AceTherm as a practical tool for thermal analysis and optimization in heterogeneous IC back-end design.
