abstract: low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are extensively utilized in triple-level cell (TLC) NAND flash memory due to their robust data error correction capability, with their performance dependent on the decoder’s iterative computation of the Log-Likelihood Ratio (LLR) messages transmitted by the NAND flash memory channel. However, implementing LDPC decoding algorithms in hardware necessitates the quantization of LLR messages due to limited hardware resources, which inevitably diminishes LLR accuracy and subsequently affects LDPC decoding performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose a classification-based graded LLR Quantization Scheme for 3D TLC NAND Flash, termed CGLLR. By employing the k-means clustering algorithm to categorize the quantized initial LLR messages from the channel, we apply distinct quantization factors to different categories of LLR values while preserving the relative magnitudes among the original LLR. This CGLLR strategy significantly enhances the resolution of LLR messages, thereby improving decoding performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CGLLR scheme reduces the average number of decoding iterations by 26.3% compared to the standard algorithm.

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have recently achieved major gains across many domains, increasing the need for hardware accelerators that can adapt to changing workloads. Because DNN layers have diverse characteristics, each may benefit from a different hardware architecture. FPGAs support this through runtime reconfiguration, but applying it to neural network accelerators remains limited. Reconfiguring the FPGA between every pair of layers would tailor hardware to each layer but incur prohibitive reconfiguration overhead. We address this by proposing a cluster-based approach that groups layers with similar computational requirements and assigns each group a shared hardware configuration. This reduces the number of reconfigurations while preserving efficient execution. However, selecting good clusters and configurations creates a large design space, especially for large networks: too few clusters merges dissimilar layers and hurts efficiency, while too many clusters increases reconfiguration overhead. To tackle this, we present a Design-Space Exploration (DSE) framework that co-optimizes clustering schemes and hardware configurations using genetic algorithms. Our method explores clustering schemes without accuracy loss, as the network and numeric precision remain fixed. Unlike prior work that optimizes only hardware or only mapping, our approach jointly optimizes both. We show that reconfiguring at carefully chosen points reduces overall inference latency despite reconfiguration costs. On GPT-2, ResNet-18, VGG01, VGG02, and AlexNet, our cluster-based designs reduce latency by 20–43% versus a fixed architecture and outperform the Simba and Eyeriss accelerators on four of five models while matching performance on VGG02.

abstract: Sequential recommendation methods are important in recommender systems, as they capture users’ dynamic interests from their historical behavior sequences. However, most existing methods have two limitations. First, they heavily rely on semantics from only a target user's interaction sequence, despite users and items with limited interactions being prevalent in real-world scenarios. Second, they suffer from popularity bias. Although data augmentation techniques have been proposed to address these issues, they struggle to augment the user with relevant and diverse data, and have limitations in dealing with popularity bias or responding to it excessively. Hence, we propose a new sequential recommendation framework that learns popularity-aware user representations via retrieval-augmentation, called REDS, to improve the quality of recommendations for users with sparse interactions and to mitigate popularity bias by: (i) incorporating embeddings of how often each item occurs in all users’ interactions into a user representation, (ii) augmenting the representation with her/his top- \(k\) similar users’ representations by leveraging the user's supervision signals during training, and (iii) disentangling the user preference into two factors to capture complementary semantics between the target user's and her/his similar users’ interaction sequences. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that REDS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The source code is available at https://github.com/JaneHubb/REDS .

abstract: Thanks to advances in the field of computer graphics and natural language processing, it is increasingly possible to create multimedia applications that use a hyper-realistic avatar as the main element of the communication interface with the user. However, major challenges remain, especially when the avatar is required to simulate the appearance and behavior of a real person. This work describes the methodology and tools necessary to create a hyper-realistic avatar that simulates the appearance and behavior of a real person. The methods and tools have been tested by developing a new application that simulates the sports training process. The design of the new application is based on the hypothesis that a digital system that hyper-realistically simulates real training can offer similar benefits to the real one and, therefore, be used to complement real training sessions and thus facilitating the continued performance of the exercise. In this work, a complete sports training simulator has been developed with special emphasis on simulating the coach's real appearance, his way of moving and speaking, as well as a personalized exercise routine generator. Finally, a between-subjects study was conducted comparing sessions led by a real coach versus his hyper-realistic digital twin. Twelve people participated in two 15-minute sessions, one with each type of coach. The analysis was performed using user experience questionnaires and physiological metrics captured through tracking bands during training sessions. The questionnaires indicated that users positively value the system as a complementary tool to their usual training routines. On the other hand, physiological metrics revealed that while users initially exert less effort with the digital avatar, their performance levels, in terms of HRV and temperature, tended to align with those of the in-person sessions halfway through the training. These findings provide valuable insights into the effectiveness and impact of digital avatars compared to real coaches in the context of fitness training.

abstract: Audio-driven 3D facial animation has emerged as a prominent research topic in computer graphics. Existing autoregressive methods are often slow and suffer from error accumulation, whereas non-autoregressive methods often struggle to establish global contextual dependencies. Moreover, current approaches remain insufficient in the cross-modal semantic alignment between audio and facial animation. To address these challenges, we propose a non-autoregressive audio-driven 3D facial animation method with multimodal context enhancement. Our method fully exploits multi-scale facial representations as well as the global contextual information within facial and audio feature sequences, enabling deep cross-modal fusion and precise semantic alignment. Specifically, we develop a global–local encoder built with spiral convolution, which facilitates complementary learning of global basic features and local fine-grained details, thereby improving the quality of facial feature extraction. We further design a multimodal context-enhanced cross-modal modulation module. This module adopts an Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN)-based cross-modal fusion strategy to modulate facial features with audio sequence context in a single step, achieving fast generation without error accumulation. In addition, the module constructs a feature region cross-attention mechanism to capture contextual dependencies within facial features, and leverages globally-aware adaptive channel weighting to model temporal contextual relations of multimodal fused features. These designs enable effective exploitation of global context and substantially improve cross-modal semantic alignment accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms mainstream baselines in both animation quality and generation efficiency.

abstract: Text-to-video retrieval answers user queries through searches based on concepts and embeddings. However, due to limitations in the size of the concept bank and the amount of training data, answering queries in the wild is not always effective because of the out-of-vocabulary problem. Furthermore, neither concept-based nor embedding-based search can perform reasoning to consolidate search results for complex queries that include logical and spatial constraints. To address these challenges, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to paraphrase queries using text-to-text (T2T), text-to-image (T2I), and image-to-text (I2T) transformations. These transformations rephrase abstract concepts into simpler terms to mitigate the out-of-vocabulary problem. Additionally, complex relationships within a query can be decomposed into simpler sub-queries, improving retrieval performance by effectively fusing the search results of these sub-queries. To mitigate the issue of LLM hallucination, this paper also proposes a novel consistency-based verification strategy to filter out factually incorrect paraphrased queries. Extensive experiments are conducted for ad-hoc video search and known-item search on the TRECVid datasets. We provide empirical insights into how traditionally difficult-to-answer queries can be effectively resolved through query paraphrasing.

abstract: Multi-modal hashing converts high-dimensional features into compact binary codes while preserving semantic similarity, thereby achieving high performance with lower storage and computational costs. However, existing methods generally overly depend on discrete supervisory information, ignoring the ambiguity of labels and intra-class diversity. To address these challenges, we propose a novel S emantic S elf-refinement M ulti-modal H ashing (SSMH), which adaptively learns stable semantic representations through a unified end-to-end semantic learning. First, we dynamically integrate inter- and intra- modal correlations to achieve semantically consistent multi-modal integrated representation. Then, we generate prototype-guided binary codes to explicitly align multi-modal representations with label semantics, thereby strengthening supervision and mitigating the effect of ambiguous labels. Extensive experiments show SSMH outperforms state-of-the-art methods in multi-modal retrieval. The source code can be found at https://github.com/vindahi/SSMH.

abstract: Multimodal aspect based sentiment analysis (MABSA) aims to infer the sentiment polarity toward a specific aspect by jointly leveraging textual and visual evidence. Despite recent progress, existing methods still suffer from three major limitations: they often rely on static shared prompts, have limited access to aspect-relevant external knowledge, and remain vulnerable when multimodal cues are noisy, incomplete, or weakly aligned with the target aspect. To address these issues, we propose RAMP , a unified framework that integrates aspect-aware retrieval, dynamic prompt generation, missing-cue compensation, hierarchical prompt encoding, and deep perturbation optimization. Specifically, RAMP first retrieves semantically relevant multimodal instances from an external memory bank to introduce aspect-aware contextual evidence beyond the current sample. It then converts the retrieved evidence into instance-specific prompts through a context-aware dynamic prompting mechanism, while adaptively compensating for unreliable or incomplete modalities. The generated prompts are further refined by a hierarchical prompt encoder and injected into multiple Transformer layers through deep perturbation, enabling shallow retrieved knowledge and deep semantic guidance to be consistently integrated. Finally, an aspect-guided aggregation module produces the sentiment prediction. Extensive experiments on Twitter-2015, Twitter-2017, and MASAD demonstrate that RAMP consistently outperforms strong baselines in both Accuracy and Macro-F1.

abstract: Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) integrates physical laws into neural network training to solve complex problems governed by differential equations. A critical component in PIML is computing derivatives of models to ensure compliance with the governing equations. A common approach is to use automatic differentiation (AD) methods available in machine learning frameworks such as PyTorch, which is accurate but not always the most efficient approach. An alternative AD method is demonstrated here in the context of physics-regularized genetic programming with symbolic regression (PR-GPSR). This work introduces Hypercomplex-based Automatic Differentiation (HYPAD), which utilizes the Order Truncated Imaginary (OTI) library to efficiently compute second- and fourth-order derivatives in PR-GPSR applications via BINGO, an open-source symbolic regression library. Numerical experiments demonstrate that HYPAD achieves up to a \(123\times\) runtime improvement over PyTorch implementations, with both approaches recovering the correct solutions in the demonstrated PR-GPSR problems. HYPAD evaluates functions by propagating OTI hypercomplex numbers through a command array representation, enabling computation of arbitrary-order derivatives. The approach may also be applicable beyond symbolic regression, motivating further investigation in other PIML and AD applications.

abstract: Precision emulation algorithms, such as the Ozaki schemes, can leverage low-precision matrix multiply–accumulate to approximate the product \(AB\) , where \(A\) and \(B\) are high-precision floating-point matrices, via fixed-point arithmetic. A key difficulty of these approaches is that achieving a target floating-point precision \(p\) requires a fixed-point bit width \(w=p+\star\) , where the required number of extra bits \(\star\) depends strongly on the matrix coefficients. The exponent span capacity (ESC), recently introduced in the literature, is an upper bound \(\overline{e}\geq\star\) . For square matrices of order \(n\) , the ESC can be estimated with \(O(n^{2}k)\) operations, where the parameter \(k\) can be increased to improve the sharpness of \(\overline{e}\) . We show that this bound can be very pessimistic, and that for the estimator to be useful, \(k\) must scale with \(n\) , effectively incurring an \(O(n^{3})\) overhead. Building on a rigorous error analysis, we then derive a new formula for \(\star\) , which corroborates the previously proposed formula up to a few bits. We propose an alternative, sharper bound, which can be computed with \(O(n^{2}k)\) operations, where \(k\) becomes independent of \(n\) . Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the current approach can substantially overestimate \(\star\) in many cases, whilst our new approach is almost perfectly sharp even for moderate values of \(k\) . We present strategies for handling matrices with zero coefficients and give a refined formulation for \(\star\) , in which different fixed-point bit widths are used for \(A\) and \(B\) . Overall, this work provides rigorous theoretical accuracy guarantees for fixed-point emulation and a practical algorithm to inexpensively yet sharply determine the required fixed-point bit width.

abstract: Missing security checks on critical variables are an important class of semantic bugs in the Linux kernel and can lead to severe vulnerabilities. Existing approaches largely rely on static analysis, but heuristic rule-based and statistical approaches may fail to capture the semantic context needed to determine whether a security check is required. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to complement static analysis with semantic reasoning. However, directly applying LLMs to kernel code remains challenging, particularly in identifying critical variables and interpreting security-check semantics. To address these challenges, we present LLMSA-MC, a framework that combines static analysis with LLM-based semantic reasoning for missing-check bug detection. LLMSA-MC incorporates three strategies: (1) Statement Type Classification, which guides LLMs to identify critical variables; (2) Precise Code Context Extraction, which provides relevant code context for semantic reasoning; and (3) Function Label Generation, which annotates function return values with semantic labels. Evaluation on curated intra- and inter-procedural benchmarks shows that LLMSA-MC improves F1-score by up to 39.01 and 33.66 percentage points, respectively, over baseline chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. When integrated with a representative missing-check bug detection tool, LLMSA-MC reduces candidate reports by 55.38% while confirming 168 missing-check bugs in Linux kernel v4.20-rc5.

abstract: Mobile Crowdsensing (MCS) faces persistent challenges in user participation, data freshness (Age of Information), privacy, and scalability in decentralized environments. We introduce HMOM-MCS , a focused framework deliberately centered on three interdependent pillars: (1) the novel Hybrid Bald Eagle Search–Gazelle Optimizer (BES-GO) that efficiently solves the non-convex, time-dependent, multi-objective incentive problem with sublinear regret \(O(\sqrt {T\log T}) \) under standard online-learning assumptions; (2) a strict mobile-edge-fog-cloud architecture that reduces decision-making latency by 30–40% while enabling real-time incentives; and (3) a participation-centric incentive suite (entry lotteries for newcomers, social referral bonuses, and reputation multipliers) that works synergistically with federated-learning-based user profiling and blockchain settlement. In simulation, and under the behavioral assumptions described in the paper, this design achieves 21–52% higher social welfare, raises the participation rate from below 60% to 85%, attains 98% task completion, lowers information latency by 16–25%, and reduces energy consumption by 20–25% compared to state-of-the-art baselines. On the theory side, we establish incentive compatibility for the VCG core augmented with bid-independent bonuses (with the scope of the remaining incentive terms delimited explicitly), individual rationality, budget feasibility, and sublinear regret under standard online-learning assumptions. Extensive simulations on real-world traces (Rome Taxi, Geolife, Foursquare, CRAWDAD) and ablation studies indicate that, under the simulation settings considered, removing any of the three pillars causes statistically significant performance degradation ( p < 0.001). These results are simulation-based: they characterize behavior under our modeling assumptions rather than measured real-world participation, and human-subject validation in a live testbed remains an essential direction for future work. All code and data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Ali-Hosseini5422/HMOM-MCS-Simulator.

abstract: Abstract Bloom filter is a widely used classic data structure for approximate membership queries. Learned Bloom filters improve memory efficiency by leveraging machine learning, with the partitioned learned Bloom filter (PLBF) being among the most memory-efficient variants. However, PLBF suffers from high construction cost, with time complexity $$\mathcal {O}(N^3k)$$ O ( N 3 k ) , where N and k are hyperparameters. In this paper, we propose three methods, fast PLBF , fast PLBF++ , and fast PLBF# , that reduce the construction complexity to $$\mathcal {O}(N^2k)$$ O ( N 2 k ) , $$\mathcal {O}(Nk \log N)$$ O ( N k log N ) , and $$\mathcal {O}(Nk \log k)$$ O ( N k log k ) , respectively. Fast PLBF preserves the original PLBF structure and memory efficiency. Although fast PLBF++ and fast PLBF# may have different structures, we theoretically prove they are equivalent to PLBF under ideal data distribution. Furthermore, for non-ideal scenarios, we introduce an instance-specific measure of deviation from the ideal distribution and use it to bound the resulting difference in memory efficiency between PLBF and fast PLBF++. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that, under the default setting ( $$N=1000$$ N = 1000 and $$k=5$$ k = 5 ), fast PLBF, fast PLBF++, and fast PLBF# are up to 58.7, 74.5, and 75.7 times faster to construct than original PLBF, respectively. In an ablation with larger k , which enables the construction of more accurate PLBFs, the speedups reach 235, 865, and 871 times at $$k=50$$ k = 50 . Additionally, fast PLBF maintains the same data structure as PLBF, and fast PLBF++ and fast PLBF# achieve nearly identical memory efficiency.

abstract: Abstract The shortest path counting is an important problem for various applications in road networks, such as traffic analysis, reliability assessment, and navigation services. Existing methods, such as 2-hop labeling schemes, precompute shortest-path distances and counts to enable fast query responses, but they face scalability challenges in large and dynamically changing networks. In this work, we propose an efficient solution, Dynamic Count Labeling (DCL) , for shortest path count queries on dynamic road networks. DCL consists of three key components: a tree hierarchy , a 2-hop count labeling scheme , and a shortcut count graph scheme . The tree hierarchy organizes the network to guide the 2-hop labeling design and ensures efficient query processing by limiting the search space to a small subset of relevant label entries. The shortcut count graph scheme enables efficient construction and dynamic maintenance of the 2-hop labels under edge weight increases and decreases. We further develop dynamic algorithms to update both the shortcut count graph and the 2-hop labels in response to network changes. Additionally, we introduce a parallel version of our algorithms that leverages the label structure for high parallel efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that DCL can compete with existing approaches for static graphs in terms of construction time, index size and query time, while enabling efficient index updates for dynamic graphs, at a fraction of reconstruction costs.

abstract: Maximizing monotone submodular functions under a matroid constraint is a classic algorithmic problem with multiple applications in data mining and machine learning. We study this significant problem in the fully dynamic setting, where elements can be both inserted and deleted in real-time. Our main result is a randomized algorithm that maintains an efficient data structure with an \({\tilde{O}(\frac{{k^{2}}}{{\varepsilon}})}\) amortized update time (in the number of insertions and deletions) and yields a \({(4+O(\varepsilon))}\) -approximate solution with respect to the dynamic optimum, where \(k\) is the rank of the matroid.

abstract: Label-specific features work as an effective supervised feature manipulation strategy to account for distinct discriminative properties of each class label in multi-label classification. Existing approaches implement this strategy in its primal form, i.e., finding the most pertinent features specific to each class label and directly inducing classifiers on these features. Instead of such a straightforward implementation, a dual perspective for label-specific feature learning is investigated in this article. As a dual problem of existing primal one, we consider label-specific discriminative properties by identifying non-informative features for each class label and making the discrimination process immutable to variations of identified features. Accordingly, a perturbation-based approach Dela is presented, which endows classifiers with immutability on simultaneously identified non-informative features by solving a probabilistically relaxed expected risk minimization problem. Furthermore, we touch the realistic issue of label-specific feature learning in a weakly supervised scenario via extending Dela to accommodate to multi-label data with missing labels. Comprehensive experiments show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art counterparts.
